q: Beggarly sins, that is, those sins which idleness and beggary usually betray men to; such as lying, flattery, stealing, and dissimulation. Jer. Taylor.

senses.d: In an indigent, mean, or despicable manner; in the manner of a beggar.
To have or commence an independent or first existence; to take rise; to commence.
q: Vast chain of being! which from God began. Pope.

senses.d: To do the first act or the first part of an action; to enter upon or commence something new, as a new form or state of being, or course of action; to take the first step; to start.
q: When I begin, I will also make an end. 1 Sam. iii. 12.

Begin.etym: [AS. beginnan (akin to OS. biginnan, D. & G. beginnen, OHG. biginnan, Goth., du-ginnan, Sw. begynna, Dan. begynde); pref. be- + an assumed ginnan. √31. See Gin to begin.]

senses.d: To enter on; to commence.
q: Ye nymphs of Solyma ! begin the song. Pope.

senses.d: To trace or lay the foundation of; to make or place a beginning of.
q: The apostle begins our knowledge in the creatures, which leads us to the knowledge of God. Locke.

Begin.syn: To commence; originate; set about; start.

senses.d: Beginning.

The act of doing that which begins anything; commencement of an action, state, or space of time; entrance into being or upon a course; the first act, effort, or state of a succession of acts or states.
q: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Gen. i. 1.

senses.d: That which begins or originates something; the first cause; origin; source.
q: I am . . . the beginning and the ending. Rev. i. 8.

senses.d: That which is begun; a rudiment or element.
q: Mighty things from small beginnings grow. Dryden.

senses.d: Enterprise.

Beginning.syn: Inception; prelude; opening; threshold; origin; outset; foundation.

senses.d: To delude by guile, artifice, or craft; to deceive or impose on, as by a false statement; to lure.
q: The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat. Gen. iii. 13.

senses.d: To elude, or evade by craft; to foil.
q: When misery could beguile the tyrant's rage. Shak.

senses.d: To cause the time of to pass without notice; to relieve the tedium or weariness of; to while away; to divert.
q: Ballads . . . to beguile his incessant wayfaring. W. Irving.

Beguile.syn: To delude; deceive; cheat; insnare; mislead; amuse; divert; entertain.

senses.d: Alluring by guile; deluding; misleading; diverting.
Advantage; favor; stead; benefit; interest; profit; support; defense; vindication.
q: In behalf of his mistress's beauty. Sir P. Sidney.
Against whom he had contracted some prejudice in behalf of his nation. Clarendon.

Behalf.etym: [OE. on-behalve in the name of, bihalven by the side of, fr. AS. healf half, also side, part: akin to G. halb half, halber on account of. See Be-, and Half, n.]

senses.d: To manage or govern in point of behavior; to discipline; to handle; to restrain.
q: He did behave his anger ere 't was spent. Shak.

senses.d: To carry; to conduct; to comport; to manage; to bear; — used reflexively.
q: Those that behaved themselves manfully. 2 Macc. ii. 21.

Behave.etym: [AS. behabban to surround, restrain, detain (akin to G. gehaben (obs.) to have, sich gehaben to behave or carry one's self); pref. be- + habban to have. See Have, v. t. ]

senses.d: To act; to conduct; to bear or carry one's self; as, to behave well or ill.
To sever the head from; to take off the head of.

Behead.etym: [OE. bihefden, AS. beheáfdian; pref. be- + heáfod head. See Head.]

senses.d: An animal, probably the hippopotamus, described in Job xl. 15-24.
On the side opposite the front or nearest part; on the back side of; at the back of; on the other side of; as, behind a door; behind a hill.
q: A tall Brabanter, behind whom I stood. Bp. Hall.

senses.d: Left after the departure of, whether this be by removing to a distance or by death.
q: A small part of what he left behind him. Pope.

senses.d: Left a distance by, in progress of improvement Hence: Inferior to in dignity, rank, knowledge, or excellence, or in any achievement.
q: I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles. 2 Cor. xi. 5.

Behind.etym: [AS. behindan; pref. be- + hindan. See Hind, a.]

senses.d: At the back part; in the rear.
Toward the back part or rear; backward; as, to look behind.
Not yet brought forward, produced, or exhibited to view; out of sight; remaining.
q: We can not be sure that there is no evidence behind. Locke.

senses.d: Backward in time or order of succession; past.
q: Forgetting those things which are behind. Phil. ii. 13.

senses.d: After the departure of another; as, to stay behind.
q: Leave not a rack behind. Shak.

senses.d: The backside; the rump.
To have in sight; to see clearly; to look at; to regard with the eyes.
q: When he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived. Num. xxi. 9.
Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world. John. i. 29.

Behold.syn: To scan; gaze; regard; descry; view; discern.
Behold.etym: [OE. bihalden, biholden, AS. behealdan to hold, have in sight; pref. be- + healdan to hold, keep; akin to G. behalten to hold, keep. See Hold.]

senses.d: To direct the eyes to, or fix them upon, an object; to look; to see.
q: And I beheld, and, lo, in the midst of the throne, . . . a lamb as it had been slain. Rev. v. 6.

senses.d: Obliged; beholden.
q: I was much bound and beholding to the right reverend father. Robynson (More's Utopia).
So much hath Oxford been beholding to her nephews, or sister's children. Fuller.

senses.d: The act of seeing; sight; also, that which is beheld.
and derivatives. See Behoove, &c.
Existing.
q: A man who is being strangled. Lamb.
While the article on Burns was being written. Froude.
Fresh experience is always being gained. Jowett (Thucyd. )

senses.d: Existence, as opposed to nonexistence; state or sphere of existence.
q: In Him we live, and move, and have our being. Acts xvii. 28.

senses.d: That which exists in any form, whether it be material or spiritual, actual or ideal; living existence, as distinguished from a thing without life; as, a human being; spiritual beings.
q: What a sweet being is an honest mind ! Beau. & Fl.
A Being of infinite benevolence and power. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Lifetime; mortal existence.
q: Claudius, thou Wast follower of his fortunes in his being. Webster (1654).

senses.d: An abode; a cottage.
q: It was a relief to dismiss them into little beings within my manor. Steele.

senses.d: Since; inasmuch as.
q: And being you have Declined his means, you have increased his malice. Beau. & Fl.

senses.d: Half a shekel.
The Babylonian name of the god known among the Hebrews as Baal. See Baal.

A thorny rutaceous tree (Ægle marmelos) of India, and its aromatic, orange-like fruit; — called also Bengal quince, golden apple, wood apple. The fruit is used medicinally, and the rind yields a perfume and a yellow dye.
To eject or throw up from the stomach with violence; to eruct.
q: I belched a hurricane of wind. Swift.

senses.d: To eject violently from within; to cast forth; to emit; to give vent to; to vent.
q: Within the gates that now Stood open wide, belching outrageous flame. Milton.

Belch.etym: [OE. belken, AS. bealcan, akin to E. bellow. See Bellow, v. i.]

senses.d: To eject wind from the stomach through the mouth; to eructate.
To issue with spasmodic force or noise.
The act of belching; also, that which is belched; an eructation.
Malt liquor; — vulgarly so called as causing eructation.
An evil spirit; a wicked and unprincipled person; the personification of evil.
q: What concord hath Christ with Belia ? 2 Cor. vi. 15.

Belial.etym: [Heb. beli ya'al; beli without + ya'al profit.]

senses.d: To show to be false; to convict of, or charge with, falsehood.
q: Their trembling hearts belie their boastful tongues. Dryden.

senses.d: To give a false representation or account of.
q: Should I do so, I should belie my thoughts. Shak.

senses.d: To tell lie about; to calumniate; to slander.
q: Thou dost belie him, Percy, thou dost belie him. Shak.

senses.d: To mimic; to counterfeit.
To fill with lies.

Belie.etym: [OE. bilien, bili�en, AS. beleógan; pref. be- + leógan to lie. See Lie, n.]

senses.d: Assent to a proposition or affirmation, or the acceptance of a fact, opinion, or assertion as real or true, without immediate personal knowledge; reliance upon word or testimony; partial or full assurance without positive knowledge or absolute certainty; persuasion; conviction; confidence; as, belief of a witness; the belief of our senses.
q: Belief admits of all degrees, from the slightest suspicion to the fullest assurance. Reid.

senses.d: A persuasion of the truths of religion; faith.
q: No man can attain belief by the bare contemplation of heaven and earth. Hooker.

senses.d: The thing believed; the object of belief.
q: Superstitious prophecies are not only the belief of fools, but the talk sometimes of wise men. Bacon.

senses.d: A tenet, or the body of tenets, held by the advocates of any class of views; doctrine; creed.
q: In the heat of persecution to which Christian belief was subject upon its first promulgation. Hooker.

Belief.etym: [OE. bileafe, bileve; cf. AS. geleáfa. See Believe.]

senses.d: To exercise belief in; to credit upon the authority or testimony of another; to be persuaded of the truth of, upon evidence furnished by reasons, arguments, and deductions of the mind, or by circumstances other than personal knowledge; to regard or accept as true; to place confidence in; to think; to consider; as, to believe a person, a statement, or a doctrine.
q: Our conqueror (whom I now Of force believe almighty). Milton.
King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets ? Acts xxvi. 27.
Often followed by a dependent clause. I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. Acts viii. 37.

Believe.etym: [OE. bileven (with pref. be- for AS. ge-), fr. AS. gel�fan, gel�fan; akin to D. gelooven, OHG. gilouban, G. glauben, OS. gil�bian, Goth. galaubjan, and Goth. liubs dear. See Lief, a., Leave, n.]

senses.d: To have a firm persuasion, esp. of the truths of religion; to have a persuasion approaching to certainty; to exercise belief or faith.
q: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. Mark ix. 24.
With the heart man believeth unto righteousness. Rom. x. 10.

senses.d: To think; to suppose.
q: I will not believe so meanly of you. Fielding.

senses.d: One who believes; one who is persuaded of the truth or reality of some doctrine, person, or thing.

One who gives credit to the truth of the Scriptures, as a revelation from God; a Christian; — in a more restricted sense, one who receives Christ as his Savior, and accepts the way of salvation unfolded in the gospel.
q: Thou didst open the Kingdom of Heaven to all believers. Book of Com. Prayer.

senses.d: One who was admitted to all the rights of divine worship and instructed in all the mysteries of the Christian religion, in distinction from a catechumen, or one yet under instruction.
That believes; having belief.
A hollow metallic vessel, usually shaped somewhat like a cup with a flaring mouth, containing a clapper or tongue, and giving forth a ringing sound on being struck.
A hollow perforated sphere of metal containing a loose ball which causes it to sound when moved.
Anything in the form of a bell, as the cup or corol of a flower.
That part of the capital of a column included between the abacus and neck molding; also used for the naked core of nearly cylindrical shape, assumed to exist within the leafage of a capital.
The strikes of the bell which mark the time; or the time so designated.

Bell.etym: [AS. belle, fr. bellan to bellow. See Bellow.]

senses.d: To put a bell upon; as, to bell the cat.
To make bell-mouthed; as, to bell a tube.
To develop bells or corollas; to take the form of a bell; to blossom; as, hops bell.
To utter by bellowing.
To call or bellow, as the deer in rutting time; to make a bellowing sound; to roar.
q: As loud as belleth wind in hell. Chaucer.
The wild buck bells from ferny brake. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To make a hollow, loud noise, as an enraged bull.
To bowl; to vociferate; to clamor.
To roar; as the sea in a tempest, or as the wind when violent; to make a loud, hollow, continued sound.
q: The bellowing voice of boiling seas. Dryden.

Bellow.etym: [OE. belwen, belowen, AS. bylgean, fr. bellan; akin to G. bellen, and perh. to L. flere to weep, OSlav. bleja to bleat, Lith. balsas voice. Cf. Bell, n. & v., Bawl, Bull.]

senses.d: To emit with a loud voice; to shout; — used with out.
A loud resounding outcry or noise, as of an enraged bull; a roar.

An instrument, utensil, or machine, which, by alternate expansion and contraction, or by rise and fall of the top, draws in air through a valve and expels it through a tube for various purposes, as blowing fires, ventilating mines, or filling the pipes of an organ with wind.

Bellows.etym: [OE. bely, below, belly, bellows, AS. bælg, bælig, bag, bellows, belly. Bellows is prop. a pl. and the orig. sense is bag. See Belly.]

senses.d: That part of the human body which extends downward from the breast to the thighs, and contains the bowels, or intestines; the abdomen.
The under part of the body of animals, corresponding to the human belly.
q: Underneath the belly of their steeds. Shak.

senses.d: The womb.
q: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee. Jer. i. 5.

senses.d: The part of anything which resembles the human belly in protuberance or in cavity; the innermost part; as, the belly of a flask, muscle, sail, ship.
q: Out of the belly of hell cried I. Jonah ii. 2.

senses.d: The hollow part of a curved or bent timber, the convex part of which is the back.

Belly.etym: [OE. bali, bely, AS. belg, bælg, bælig, bag, bellows, belly; akin to Icel. belgr bag, bellows, Sw. bälg, Dan. bælg, D. & G. balg, cf. W. bol the paunch or belly, dim. boly, Ir. bolg. Cf. Bellows, Follicle, Fool, Bilge.]

senses.d: To cause to swell out; to fill.
q: Your breath of full consent bellied his sails. Shak.

senses.d: To swell and become protuberant, like the belly; to bulge.
q: The bellying canvas strutted with the gale. Dryden.

senses.d: To be the property of; as, Jamaica belongs to Great Britain.
To be a part of, or connected with; to be appendant or related; to owe allegiance or service.
q: A desert place belonging to . . . Bethsaids. Luke ix. 10.
The mighty men which belonged to David. 1 Kings i. 8.

senses.d: To be the concern or proper business or function of; to appertain to.
To be suitable for; to be due to.
q: Strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age. Heb. v. 14.
No blame belongs to thee. Shak.

senses.d: To be native to, or an inhabitant of; esp. to have a legal residence, settlement, or inhabitancy, whether by birth or operation of law, so as to be entitled to maintenance by the parish or town.
q: Bastards also are settled in the parishes to which the mothers belong. Blackstone.

Belong.etym: [OE. belongen (akin to D. belangen to concern, G. belangen to attain to, to concern); pref. be- + longen to desire. See Long, v. i.]

senses.d: To be deserved by.
q: More evils belong us than happen to us. B. Jonson.

senses.d: That which belongs to one; that which pertains to one; hence, goods or effects.
That which is connected with a principal or greater thing; an appendage; an appurtenance.
Family; relations; household.
q: Few persons of her ladyship's belongings stopped, before they did her bidding, to ask her reasons. Thackeray.

senses.d: To love.

Belove.etym: [OE. bilufien. See pref. Be-, and Love, v. t.]

senses.d: Greatly loved; dear to the heart.
q: Antony, so well beloved of Cæsar. Shak.
This is my beloved Son. Matt. iii. 17.

senses.d: One greatly loved.
q: My beloved is mine, and I am his. Cant. ii. 16.

senses.d: To express deep grief for by moaning; to express sorrow for; to lament; to bewail; to pity or sympathize with.
q: Implores their pity, and his pain bemoans. Dryden.

Bemoan.etym: [OE. bimenen, AS. bem�nan; pref. be- + m�nan to moan. See Moan.]

senses.d: The seed of one or more species of moringa; as, oil of ben. See Moringa.
Within; in; in or into the interior; toward the inner apartment.

Ben.etym: [AS. binnan; pref. be- by + innan within, in in.]

senses.d: The inner or principal room in a hut or house of two rooms; — opposed to but, the outer apartment.
An old form of the pl. indic. pr. of Be.
A long seat, differing from a stool in its greater length.
q: Mossy benches supplied the place of chairs. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A long table at which mechanics and other work; as, a carpenter's bench.
The seat where judges sit in court.
q: To pluck down justice from your awful bench. Shak.

senses.d: The persons who sit as judges; the court; as, the opinion of the full bench. See King's Bench.
A collection or group of dogs exhibited to the public; — so named because the animals are usually placed on benches or raised platforms.
A conformation like a bench; a long stretch of flat ground, or a kind of natural terrace, near a lake or river.

Bench.etym: [OE. bench, benk, AS. benc; akin to Sw. bänk, Dan bænk, Icel. bekkr, OS., D., & G. bank. Cf. Bank, Beach.]

senses.d: To furnish with benches.
q: 'T was benched with turf. Dryden.
Stately theaters benched crescentwise. Tennyson.

senses.d: To place on a bench or seat of honor.
q: Whom I . . . have benched and reared to worship. Shak.

senses.d: To sit on a seat of justice.
To strain or move out of a straight line; to crook by straining; to make crooked; to curve; to make ready for use by drawing into a curve; as, to bend a bow; to bend the knee.
To turn toward some certain point; to direct; to incline.
q: Towards Coventry bend we our course. Shak.
Bending her eyes . . . upon her parent. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To apply closely or with interest; to direct.
q: To bend his mind to any public business. Temple.
But when to mischief mortals bend their will. Pope.

senses.d: To cause to yield; to render submissive; to subdue.
To fasten, as one rope to another, or as a sail to its yard or stay; or as a cable to the ring of an anchor.

Bend.syn: To lean; stoop; deflect; bow; yield.
Bend.etym: [AS. bendan to bend, fr. bend a band, bond, fr. bindan to bind. See Bind, v. t., and cf. 3d & 4th Bend.]

senses.d: To be moved or strained out of a straight line; to crook or be curving; to bow.
q: The green earth's end Where the bowed welkin slow doth bend. Milton.

senses.d: To jut over; to overhang.
q: There is a cliff, whose high and bending head Looks fearfully in the confined deep. Shak.

senses.d: To be inclined; to be directed.
q: To whom our vows and wished bend. Milton.

senses.d: To bow in prayer, or in token of submission.
q: While each to his great Father bends. Coleridge.

senses.d: A turn or deflection from a straight line or from the proper direction or normal position; a curve; a crook; as, a slight bend of the body; a bend in a road.
Turn; purpose; inclination; ends.
q: Farewell, poor swain; thou art not for my bend. Fletcher.

senses.d: A knot by which one rope is fastened to another or to an anchor, spar, or post.
The best quality of sole leather; a butt. See Butt.
Hard, indurated clay; bind.
same as caisson disease. Usually referred to as the bends.

Bend.etym: [See Bend, v. t., and cf. Bent, n.]

senses.d: A band.
One of the honorable ordinaries, containing a third or a fifth part of the field. It crosses the field diagonally from the dexter chief to the sinister base.

Bend.etym: [AS. bend. See Band, and cf. the preceding noun.]

senses.d: The marking of the clothes with stripes or horizontal bands.
A prayer; boon.
q: What is good for a bootless bene ? Wordsworth.

senses.d: A hoglike mammal of New Guinea (Porcula papuensis).
Lower in place, with something directly over or on; under; underneath; hence, at the foot of.
q: Beneath a rude and nameless stone he lies. Pope.

senses.d: Under, in relation to something that is superior, or that oppresses or burdens.
q: Our country sinks beneath the yoke. Shak.

senses.d: Lower in rank, dignity, or excellence than; as, brutes are beneath man; man is beneath angels in the scale of beings. Hence: Unworthy of; unbecoming.
q: He will do nothing that is beneath his high station. Atterbury.

Beneath.etym: [OE. benethe, bineoðen, AS. beneoðan, benyðan; pref. be- + neoðan, nyðan, downward, beneath, akin to E. nether. See Nether.]

senses.d: In a lower place; underneath.
q: The earth you take from beneath will be barren. Mortimer.

senses.d: Below, as opposed to heaven, or to any superior region or position; as, in earth beneath.
One who confers a benefit or benefits.
An act of kindness; a favor conferred.
q: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits. Ps. ciii. 2.

senses.d: Whatever promotes prosperity and personal happiness, or adds value to property; advantage; profit.
q: Men have no right to what is not for their benefit. Burke.

senses.d: A theatrical performance, a concert, or the like, the proceeds of which do not go to the lessee of the theater or to the company, but to some individual actor, or to some charitable use.
Beneficence; liberality.
Natural advantages; endowments; accomplishments.

Benefit.syn: Profit; service; use; avail. See Advantage.
Benefit.etym: [OE. benefet, benfeet, bienfet, F. bienfait, fr. L. benefactum; bene well (adv. of bonus good) + factum, p. p. of facere to do. See Bounty, and Fact.]

senses.d: To be beneficial to; to do good to; to advantage; to advance in health or prosperity; to be useful to; to profit.
q: I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them. Jer. xviii. 10.

senses.d: To gain advantage; to make improvement; to profit; as, he will benefit by the change.
The disposition to do good; good will; charitableness; love of mankind, accompanied with a desire to promote their happiness.
q: The wakeful benevolence of the gospel. Chalmers.

senses.d: An act of kindness; good done; charity given.
A species of compulsory contribution or tax, which has sometimes been illegally exacted by arbitrary kings of England, and falsely represented as a gratuity.
A kind of upper coat for men.
A descendant of Benjamin; one of the tribe of Benjamin.
Changed by pressure so as to be no longer straight; crooked; as, a bent pin; a bent lever.

Strongly inclined toward something, so as to be resolved, determined, set, etc.; — said of the mind, character, disposition, desires, etc., and used with on; as, to be bent on going to college; he is bent on mischief.
The state of being curved, crooked, or inclined from a straight line; flexure; curvity; as, the bent of a bow.
A declivity or slope, as of a hill.
A leaning or bias; proclivity; tendency of mind; inclination; disposition; purpose; aim.
q: With a native bent did good pursue. Dryden.

senses.d: Particular direction or tendency; flexion; course.
q: Bents and turns of the matter. Locke.

senses.d: A transverse frame of a framed structure.
Tension; force of acting; energy; impetus.
q: The full bent and stress of the soul. Norris.

senses.d: A reedlike grass; a stalk of stiff, coarse grass.
q: His spear a bent, both stiff and strong. Drayton.

senses.d: A grass of the genus Agrostis, esp. Agrostis vulgaris, or redtop. The name is also used of many other grasses, esp. in America.
Any neglected field or broken ground; a common; a moor.
q: Bowmen bickered upon the bent. Chevy Chase.

Bent.etym: [AS. beonet; akin to OHG. pinuz, G. binse, rush, bent grass; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To pierce.
To make destitute; to deprive; to strip; — with of before the person or thing taken away.
q: Madam, you have bereft me of all words. Shak.
Bereft of him who taught me how to sing. Tickell.

senses.d: To take away from.
q: All your interest in those territories Is utterly bereft you; all is lost. Shak.

senses.d: To take away.
q: Shall move you to bereave my life. Marlowe.

Bereave.etym: [OE. bireven, AS. bereáfian. See Be-, and Reave.]

senses.d: Any small fleshy fruit, as the strawberry, mulberry, huckleberry, etc.
A small fruit that is pulpy or succulent throughout, having seeds loosely imbedded in the pulp, as the currant, grape, blueberry.
The coffee bean.
One of the ova or eggs of a fish.

Berry.etym: [OE. berie, AS. berie, berige; akin to D. bes, G. beere, OS. and OHG. beri, Icel. ber, Sw. bär, Goth. basi, and perh. Skr. bhas to eat.]

senses.d: To bear or produce berries.
A mound; a hillock.

A mineral of great hardness, and, when transparent, of much beauty. It occurs in hexagonal prisms, commonly of a green or bluish green color, but also yellow, pink, and white. It is a silicate of aluminium and glucinum (beryllium). The aquamarine is a transparent, sea-green variety used as a gem. The emerald is another variety highly prized in jewelry, and distinguished by its deep color, which is probably due to the presence of a little oxide of chromium.

Beryl.etym: [F. béryl, OF. beril, L. beryllus, Gr. βήρυλλοσ, prob. fr. Skr. vaiḍūrya. Cf. Brilliant.]

senses.d: To ask or entreat with urgency; to supplicate; to implore.
q: I beseech you, punish me not with your hard thoughts. Shak.
But Eve . . . besought his peace. Milton.

Beseech.etym: [OE. bisechen, biseken (akin to G. besuchen to visit); pref. be- + sechen, seken, to seek. See Seek.]

senses.d: Solicitation; supplication.
Entreating urgently; imploring; as, a beseeching look.
To set or stud (anything) with ornaments or prominent objects.
q: A robe of azure beset with drops of gold. Spectator.
The garden is so beset with all manner of sweet shrubs that it perfumes the air. Evelyn.

senses.d: To hem in; to waylay; to surround; to besiege; to blockade.
q: Let thy troops beset our gates. Addison.

senses.d: To set upon on all sides; to perplex; to harass; — said of dangers, obstacles, etc.
To occupy; to employ; to use up.

Beset.syn: To surround; inclose; environ; hem in; besiege; encircle; encompass; embarrass; urge; press.
Beset.etym: [AS. besettan (akin to OHG. bisazjan, G. besetzen, D. bezetten); pref. be- + settan to set. See Set.]

senses.d: At the side of; on one side of.
Aside from; out of the regular course or order of; in a state of deviation from; out of.
q: have done enough To put him quite beside his patience. Shak.

senses.d: Over and above; distinct from; in addition to.
q: Wise and learned men beside those whose names are in the Christian records. Addison.
Paul, thou art beside thyself.

Beside.etym: [OE. biside, bisiden, bisides, prep. and adv., beside, besides; pref. be- by + side. Cf. Besides, and see Side, n.]

senses.d: On one side.
More than that; over and above; not included in the number, or in what has been mentioned; moreover; in addition.
q: The men said unto Lot, Hast thou here any besides ? Gen. xix. 12.
To all beside, as much an empty shade, An Eugene living, as a Cæsar dead. Pope.

Besides.etym: [OE. Same as beside, prep.; the ending -s is an adverbial one, prop. a genitive sign.]

senses.d: Over and above; separate or distinct from; in addition to; other than; else than. See Beside, prep., 3, and Syn. under Beside.
q: Besides your cheer, you shall have sport. Shak.

senses.d: To beset or surround with armed forces, for the purpose of compelling to surrender; to lay siege to; to beleaguer; to beset.
q: Till Paris was besieged, famished, and lost. Shak.

Besiege.syn: To environ; hem in; invest; encompass.
Besiege.etym: [OE. bisegen; pref. be- + segen to siege. See Siege.]

senses.d: A brush of twigs for sweeping; a broom; anything which sweeps away or destroys.
q: I will sweep it with the besom of destruction. Isa. xiv. 23.
The housemaid with her besom. W. Irving.

Besom.etym: [OE. besme, besum, AS. besma; akin to D. bezem, OHG pesamo, G. besen; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To sweep, as with a besom.
q: Rolls back all Greece, and besoms wide the plain. Barlow.

senses.d: Having good qualities in the highest degree; most good, kind, desirable, suitable, etc.; most excellent; as, the best man; the best road; the best cloth; the best abilities.
q: When he is best, he is a little worse than a man. Shak.
Heaven's last, best gift, my ever new delight. Milton.

senses.d: Most advanced; most correct or complete; as, the best scholar; the best view of a subject.
Most; largest; as, the best part of a week.

Best.etym: [AS. besta, best, contr. from betest, betst, betsta; akin to Goth. batists, OHG. pezzisto, G. best, beste, D. best, Icel. beztr, Dan. best, Sw. bäst. This word has no connection in origin with good. See Better.]

senses.d: Utmost; highest endeavor or state; most nearly perfect thing, or being, or action; as, to do one's best; to the best of our ability.
In the highest degree; beyond all others.
q: He prayeth best, who loveth best All things both great and small. Coleridge.

senses.d: To the most advantage; with the most success, case, profit, benefit, or propriety.
q: Had we best retire? I see a storm. Milton.
Had I not best go to her? Thackeray.

senses.d: Most intimately; most thoroughly or correctly; as, what is expedient is best known to himself.
To get the better of.
To put in a certain situation or condition; to circumstance; to place.
q: They shall pass through it, hardly bestead and hungry: . . . and curse their king and their God. Is. viii. 21.
Many far worse bestead than ourselves. Barrow.

senses.d: To put in peril; to beset.
To serve; to assist; to profit; to avail.
To put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigor; — usually with the reciprocal pronoun.
q: You have so bestirred your valor. Shak.
Rouse and bestir themselves ere well awake. Milton.

senses.d: To lay up in store; to deposit for safe keeping; to stow; to place; to put.
q: See that the women are bestowed in safety. Byron.

senses.d: To use; to apply; to devote, as time or strength in some occupation.
To expend, as money.
To give or confer; to impart; — with on or upon.
q: Empire is on us bestowed. Cowper.
Though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor. 1 Cor. xiii. 3.

senses.d: To give in marriage.
q: I could have bestowed her upon a fine gentleman. Tatler.

senses.d: To demean; to conduct; to behave; — followed by a reflexive pronoun.
q: How might we see Falstaff bestow himself to-night in his true colors, and not ourselves be seen ? Shak.

Bestow.syn: To give; grant; present; confer; accord.
Bestow.etym: [OE. bestowen; pref. be- + stow a place. See Stow.]

senses.d: That which is laid, staked, or pledged, as between two parties, upon the event of a contest or any contingent issue; the act of giving such a pledge; a wager.

Bet.etym: [Prob. from OE. abet abetting, OF. abet, fr. abeter to excite, incite. See Abet.]

senses.d: To stake or pledge upon the event of a contingent issue; to wager.
q: John a Gaunt loved him well, and betted much money on his head. Shak.
I'll bet you two to one I'll make him do it. O. W. Holmes.

senses.d: An early form of Better.

To call to mind; to recall or bring to recollection, reflection, or consideration; to think; to consider; — generally followed by a reflexive pronoun, often with of or that before the subject of thought.
q: I have bethought me of another fault. Shak.
The rest . . . may . . . bethink themselves, and recover. Milton.
We bethink a means to break it off. Shak.

Bethink.etym: [AS. beþencan; pref. be- + þencan to think. See Think.]

senses.d: To think; to recollect; to consider.
A hospital for lunatics; — corrupted into bedlam.
In the Ethiopic church, a small building attached to a church edifice, in which the bread for the eucharist is made.

Bethlehem.etym: [Heb. bēth-lekhem house of food; bēth house + lekhem food, lākham to eat. Formerly the name of a hospital for the insane, in London, which had been the priory of St. Mary of Bethlehem. Cf. Bedlam.]

senses.d: In good season or time; before it is late; seasonably; early.
q: To measure life learn thou betimes. Milton.
To rise betimes is often harder than to do all the day's work. Barrow.

senses.d: In a short time; soon; speedily; forth with.
q: He tires betimes that spurs too fast betimes. Shak.

Betime.etym: [Pref. be- (for by) + time; that is, by the proper time. The -s is an adverbial ending.]

senses.d: To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust; to give up treacherously or faithlessly; as, an officer betrayed the city.
q: Jesus said unto them, The Son of man shall be betrayed into the hands of men. Matt. xvii. 22.

senses.d: To prove faithless or treacherous to, as to a trust or one who trusts; to be false to; to deceive; as, to betray a person or a cause.
q: But when I rise, I shall find my legs betraying me. Johnson.

senses.d: To violate the confidence of, by disclosing a secret, or that which one is bound in honor not to make known.
q: Willing to serve or betray any government for hire. Macaulay.

senses.d: To disclose or discover, as something which prudence would conceal; to reveal unintentionally.
q: Be swift to hear, but cautious of your tongue, lest you betray your ignorance. T. Watts.

senses.d: To mislead; to expose to inconvenience not foreseen to lead into error or sin.
q: Genius . . . often betrays itself into great errors. T. Watts.

senses.d: To lead astray, as a maiden; to seduce (as under promise of marriage) and then abandon.
To show or to indicate; — said of what is not obvious at first, or would otherwise be concealed.
q: All the names in the country betray great antiquity. Bryant.

Betray.etym: [OE. betraien, bitraien; pref. be- + OF. traïr to betray, F. trahir, fr. L. tradere. See Traitor.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, betrays.
To contract to any one for a marriage; to engage or promise in order to marriage; to affiance; — used esp. of a woman.
q: He, in the first flower of my freshest age, Betrothed me unto the only heir. Spenser.
Ay, and we are betrothed. Shak.

senses.d: To promise to take (as a future spouse); to plight one's troth to.
q: What man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? Deut. xx. 7.

senses.d: To nominate to a bishopric, in order to consecration.

Betroth.etym: [Pref. be- + troth, i.e., truth. See Truth.]

senses.d: Having good qualities in a greater degree than another; as, a better man; a better physician; a better house; a better air.
q: Could make the worse appear The better reason. Milton.

senses.d: Preferable in regard to rank, value, use, fitness, acceptableness, safety, or in any other respect.
q: To obey is better than sacrifice. 1 Sam. xv. 22.
It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in princes. Ps. cxviii. 9.

senses.d: Greater in amount; larger; more.
Improved in health; less affected with disease; as, the patient is better.
More advanced; more perfect; as, upon better acquaintance; a better knowledge of the subject.

Better.etym: [OE. betere, bettre, and as adv. bet, AS. betera, adj., and bet, adv.; akin to Icel. betri, adj., betr, adv., Goth. batiza, adj., OHG. bezziro, adj., baz, adv., G. besser, adj. and adv., bass, adv., E. boot, and prob. to Skr. bhadra excellent. See Boot advantage, and cf. Best, Batful.]

senses.d: Advantage, superiority, or victory; — usually with of; as, to get the better of an enemy.
One who has a claim to precedence; a superior, as in merit, social standing, etc.; — usually in the plural.
q: Their betters would hardly be found. Hooker.

senses.d: In a superior or more excellent manner; with more skill and wisdom, courage, virtue, advantage, or success; as, Henry writes better than John; veterans fight better than recruits.
q: I could have better spared a better man. Shak.

senses.d: More correctly or thoroughly.
q: The better to understand the extent of our knowledge. Locke.

senses.d: In a higher or greater degree; more; as, to love one better than another.
q: Never was monarch better feared, and loved. Shak.

senses.d: More, in reference to value, distance, time, etc.; as, ten miles and better.
To improve or ameliorate; to increase the good qualities of.
q: Love betters what is best. Wordsworth.
He thought to better his circumstances. Thackeray.

senses.d: To improve the condition of, morally, physically, financially, socially, or otherwise.
q: The constant effort of every man to better himself. Macaulay.

senses.d: To surpass in excellence; to exceed; to excel.
q: The works of nature do always aim at that which can not be bettered. Hooker.

senses.d: To give advantage to; to support; to advance the interest of.
q: Weapons more violent, when next we meet, May serve to better us and worse our foes. Milton.

Better.syn: To improve; meliorate; ameliorate; mend; amend; correct; emend; reform; advance; promote.
Better.etym: [AS. beterian, betrian, fr. betera better. See Better, a.]

senses.d: To become better; to improve.
One who bets or lays a wager.
In the space which separates; betwixt; as, New York is between Boston and Philadelphia.
Used in expressing motion from one body or place to another; from one to another of two.
q: If things should go so between them. Bacon.

senses.d: Belonging in common to two; shared by both.
q: Castor and Pollux with only one soul between them. Locke.

senses.d: Belonging to, or participated in by, two, and involving reciprocal action or affecting their mutual relation; as, opposition between science and religion.
q: An intestine struggle, open or secret, between authority and liberty. Hume.

senses.d: With relation to two, as involved in an act or attribute of which another is the agent or subject; as, to judge between or to choose between courses; to distinguish between you and me; to mediate between nations.
In intermediate relation to, in respect to time, quantity, or degree; as, between nine and ten o'clock.

Between.etym: [OE. bytwene, bitweonen, AS. betweónan, betweónum; prefix be- by + a form fr. AS. twā two, akin to Goth. tweihnai two apiece. See Twain, and cf. Atween, Betwixt.]

senses.d: Intermediate time or space; interval.
In the space which separates; between.
q: From betwixt two aged oaks. Milton.

senses.d: From one to another of; mutually affecting.
q: There was some speech of marriage Betwixt myself and her. Shak.

Betwixt.etym: [OE. betwix, bitwix, rarely bitwixt, AS. betweox, betweohs, betweoh, betwīh; pref. be- by + a form fr. AS. twā two. See Between.]

senses.d: To express deep sorrow for, as by wailing; to lament; to wail over.
q: Hath widowed and unchilded many a one, Which to this hour bewail the injury. Shak.

senses.d: To express grief; to lament.
To be on one's guard; to be cautious; to take care; — commonly followed by of or lest before the thing that is to be avoided.
q: Beware of all, but most beware of man ! Pope.
Beware the awful avalanche. Longfellow.

senses.d: To have a special regard; to heed.
q: Behold, I send an Angel before thee. . . . Beware of him, and obey his voice. Ex. xxiii. 20, 21.

Beware.etym: [Be, imperative of verb to be + ware. See Ware, Wary.]

senses.d: To avoid; to take care of; to have a care for.
q: To wish them beware the son. Milton.

senses.d: To gain an ascendency over by charms or incantations; to affect (esp. to injure) by witchcraft or sorcery.
q: See how I am bewitched; behold, mine arm Is like a blasted sapling withered up. Shak.

senses.d: To charm; to fascinate; to please to such a degree as to take away the power of resistance; to enchant.
q: The charms of poetry our souls bewitch. Dryden.

senses.d: To soil. See Beray.
To expose; to reveal; to disclose; to betray.
q: The murder being once done, he is in less fear, and in more hope that the deed shall not be bewrayed or known. Robynson (More's Utopia. )
Thy speech bewrayeth thee. Matt. xxvi. 73.

Bewray.etym: [OE. bewraien, biwreyen; pref. be- + AS. wrēgan to accuse, betray; akin to OS. wrōgian, OHG. ruogēn, G. rügen, Icel. rægja, Goth. wrōhjan to accuse.]

senses.d: On the further side of; in the same direction as, and further on or away than.
q: Beyond that flaming hill. G. Fletcher.

senses.d: At a place or time not yet reached; before.
q: A thing beyond us, even before our death. Pope.

senses.d: Past, out of the reach or sphere of; further than; greater than; as, the patient was beyond medical aid; beyond one's strength.
In a degree or amount exceeding or surpassing; proceeding to a greater degree than; above, as in dignity, excellence, or quality of any kind.
q: Beyond any of the great men of my country. Sir P. Sidney.
That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter. 1 Thess. iv. 6.

Beyond.etym: [OE. biyonde, bi”eonde, AS. begeondan, prep. and adv.; pref. be- + geond yond, yonder. See Yon, Yonder.]

senses.d: Further away; at a distance; yonder.
q: Lo, where beyond he lyeth languishing. Spenser.

senses.d: To make an offer of; to propose. Specifically : To offer to pay ( a certain price, as for a thing put up at auction), or to take (a certain price, as for work to be done under a contract).
To offer in words; to declare, as a wish, a greeting, a threat, or defiance, etc.; as, to bid one welcome; to bid good morning, farewell, etc.
q: Neither bid him God speed. 2. John 10.
He bids defiance to the gaping crowd. Granrille.

senses.d: To proclaim; to declare publicly; to make known.
To order; to direct; to enjoin; to command.
q: That Power who bids the ocean ebb and flow. Pope
Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee. Matt. xiv. 28
I was bid to pick up shells. D. Jerrold.

senses.d: To invite; to call in; to request to come.
q: As many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage. Matt. xxii. 9

Bid.syn: To offer; proffer; tender; propose; order; command; direct; charge; enjoin.
Bid.etym: [OE. bidden, prop to ask, beg, AS. biddan; akin to OS. biddian, Icel. biðja, OHG. bittan, G. bitten, to pray, ask, request, and E. bead, also perh. to Gr. τειθειν to persuade, L. fidere to trust, E. faith, and bide. But this word was early confused with OE. beden, beoden, AS. beódan, to offer, comma

senses.d: An offer of a price, especially at auctions; a statement of a sum which one will give for something to be received, or will take for something to be done or furnished; that which is offered.
To pray.
To make a bid; to state what one will pay or take.
Command; order; a proclamation or notifying.
The act or process of making bids; an offer; a proposal of a price, as at an auction.
A handbarrow or portable frame on which a corpse is placed or borne to the grave.
A count of forty threads in the warp or chain of woolen cloth.

Bier.etym: [OE. bæe, beere, AS. b�r, b�re; akin to D. baar, OHG. bāra, G. bahre, Icel barar, D� baare, L. feretrum, Gr. �, from the same �� bear to produce. See 1st Bear, and cf. Barrow.]

senses.d: A beak, as of a bird, or sometimes of a turtle or other animal.

Bill.etym: [OE. bile, bille, AS. bile beak of a bird, proboscis; cf. Ir. & Gael. bil, bile, mouth, lip, bird's bill. Cf. Bill a weapon.]

senses.d: To strike; to peck.
To join bills, as doves; to caress in fondness.
The bell, or boom, of the bittern
q: The bittern's hollow bill was heard. Wordsworth.

senses.d: A cutting instrument, with hook-shaped point, and fitted with a handle; — used in pruning, etc.; a billhook. When short, called a hand bill, when long, a hedge bill.

A weapon of infantry, in the 14th and 15th centuries. A common form of bill consisted of a broad, heavy, double-edged, hook-shaped blade, having a short pike at the back and another at the top, and attached to the end of a long staff.
q: France had no infantry that dared to face the English bows end bills. Macaulay.

senses.d: One who wields a bill; a billman.
A pickax, or mattock.
The extremity of the arm of an anchor; the point of or beyond the fluke.

Bill.etym: [OE. bil, AS. bill, bil; akin to OS. bil sword, OHG. bill pickax, G. bille. Cf. Bill bea�.]

senses.d: To work upon ( as to dig, hoe, hack, or chop anything) with a bill.
A declaration made in writing, stating some wrong the complainant has suffered from the defendant, or a fault committed by some person against a law.
A writing binding the signer or signers to pay a certain sum at a future day or on demand, with or without interest, as may be stated in the document.
A form or draft of a law, presented to a legislature for enactment; a proposed or projected law.
A paper, written or printed, and posted up or given away, to advertise something, as a lecture, a play, or the sale of goods; a placard; a poster; a handbill.
q: She put up the bill in her parlor window. Dickens.

senses.d: An account of goods sold, services rendered, or work done, with the price or charge; a statement of a creditor's claim, in gross or by items; as, a grocer's bill.
Any paper, containing a statement of particulars; as, a bill of charges or expenditures; a weekly bill of mortality; a bill of fare, etc.

Bill.etym: [OE. bill, bille, fr. LL. billa (or OF. bille), for L. bulla anything rounded, LL., seal, stamp, letter, edict, roll; cf. F. bille a ball, prob. fr. Ger.; cf. MHG. bickel, D. bikkel, dice. Cf. Bull papal edict, Billet a paper.]

senses.d: To advertise by a bill or public notice.
To charge or enter in a bill; as, to bill goods.
A great wave or surge of the sea or other water, caused usually by violent wind.
q: Whom the winds waft where'er the billows roll. Cowper.

senses.d: A great wave or flood of anything.

Billow.etym: [Cf. Icel. bylgja billow, Dan. bölge, Sw. bölja; akin to MHG. bulge billow, bag, and to E. bulge. See Bulge.]

senses.d: To surge; to rise and roll in waves or surges; to undulate.
To tie, or confine with a cord, band, ligature, chain, etc.; to fetter; to make fast; as, to bind grain in bundles; to bind a prisoner.
To confine, restrain, or hold by physical force or influence of any kind; as, attraction binds the planets to the sun; frost binds the earth, or the streams.
q: He bindeth the floods from overflowing. Job xxviii. 11.
Whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years. Luke xiii. 16.

senses.d: To cover, as with a bandage; to bandage or dress; — sometimes with up; as, to bind up a wound.
To make fast ( a thing) about or upon something, as by tying; to encircle with something; as, to bind a belt about one; to bind a compress upon a part.
To prevent or restrain from customary or natural action; as, certain drugs bind the bowels.
To protect or strengthen by a band or binding, as the edge of a carpet or garment.
To sew or fasten together, and inclose in a cover; as, to bind a book.

Fig.: To oblige, restrain, or hold, by authority, law, duty, promise, vow, affection, or other moral tie; as, to bind the conscience; to bind by kindness; bound by affection; commerce binds nations to each other.
q: Who made our laws to bind us, not himself. Milton.

senses.d: To bring (any one) under definite legal obligations; esp. under the obligation of a bond or covenant.

Bind.syn: To fetter; tie; fasten; restrain; restrict; oblige.
Bind.etym: [AS. bindan, perfect tense band, bundon, p. p. bunden; akin to D. & G. binden, Dan. binde, Sw. & Icel. binda, Goth. bindan, Skr. bandh (for bhandh) to bind, cf. Gr. � (for �) cable, and L. offendix. √90.]

senses.d: To tie; to confine by any ligature.
q: They that reap must sheaf and bind. Shak.

senses.d: To contract; to grow hard or stiff; to cohere or stick together in a mass; as, clay binds by heat.
To be restrained from motion, or from customary or natural action, as by friction.
To exert a binding or restraining influence.
That which binds or ties.
Any twining or climbing plant or stem, esp. a hop vine; a bine.
Indurated clay, when much mixed with the oxide of iron.
A ligature or tie for grouping notes.
That binds; obligatory.

Binding.syn: Obligatory; restraining; restrictive; stringent; astringent; costive; styptic.

senses.d: The act or process of one who, or that which, binds.
Anything that binds; a bandage; the cover of a book, or the cover with the sewing, etc.; something that secures the edge of cloth from raveling.
The transoms, knees, beams, keelson, and other chief timbers used for connecting and strengthening the parts of a vessel.
Orig., a chicken; the young of a fowl; a young eaglet; a nestling; and hence, a feathered flying animal (see 2).
q: That ungentle gull, the cuckoo's bird. Shak.
The brydds of the aier have nestes. Tyndale (Matt. viii. 20).

senses.d: A warm-blooded, feathered vertebrate provided with wings. See Aves.
Specifically, among sportsmen, a game bird.
Fig.: A girl; a maiden.
q: And by my word! the bonny bird In danger shall not tarry. Campbell.

Bird.etym: [OE. brid, bred, bird, young bird, bird, AS. bridd young bird. √92.]

senses.d: To catch or shoot birds.
Hence: To seek for game or plunder; to thieve.
The act or fact of coming into life, or of being born; — generally applied to human beings; as, the birth of a son.
Lineage; extraction; descent; sometimes, high birth; noble extraction.
q: Elected without reference to birth, but solely for qualifications. Prescott.

senses.d: The condition to which a person is born; natural state or position; inherited disposition or tendency.
q: A foe by birth to Troy's unhappy name. Dryden.

senses.d: The act of bringing forth; as, she had two children at a birth.
That which is born; that which is produced, whether animal or vegetable.
q: Poets are far rarer births than kings. B. Jonson.
Others hatch their eggs and tend the birth till it is able to shift for itself. Addison.

senses.d: Origin; beginning; as, the birth of an empire.

Birth.etym: [OE. burth, birth, AS. beorð, gebyrd, fr. beran to bear, bring forth; akin to D. geboorte, OHG. burt, giburt, G. geburt, Icel. burðr, Skr. bhrti bearing, supporting; cf. Ir. & Gael. beirthe born, brought forth. √92. See 1st Bear, and cf. Berth.]

senses.d: The day in which any person is born; day of origin or commencement.
q: Those barbarous ages past, succeeded next The birthday of invention. Cowper.

senses.d: The day of the month in which a person was born, in whatever succeeding year it may recur; the anniversary of one's birth.
q: This is my birthday; as this very day Was Cassius born. Shak.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the day of birth, or its anniversary; as, birthday gifts or festivities.

Any right, privilege, or possession to which a person is entitled by birth, such as an estate descendible by law to an heir, or civil liberty under a free constitution; esp. the rights or inheritance of the first born.
q: Lest there be any . . . profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. Heb. xii. 16.

senses.d: A spiritual overseer, superintendent, or director.
q: Ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls. 1 Pet. ii. 25.

It is a fact now generally recognized by theologians of all shades of opinion, that in the language of the New Testament the same officer in the church is called indifferently “bishop” ( � ) and “elder” or “presbyter.” J. B. Lightfoot.

senses.d: In the Roman Catholic, Greek, and Anglican or Protestant Episcopal churches, one ordained to the highest order of the ministry, superior to the priesthood, and generally claiming to be a successor of the Apostles. The bishop is usually the spiritual head or ruler of a diocese, bishopric, or see.
In the Methodist Episcopal and some other churches, one of the highest church officers or superintendents.
A piece used in the game of chess, bearing a representation of a bishop's miter; — formerly called archer.
A beverage, being a mixture of wine, oranges or lemons, and sugar.
An old name for a woman's bustle.
q: If, by her bishop, or her “grace” alone, A genuine lady, or a church, is known. Saxe.

Bishop.etym: [OE. bischop, biscop, bisceop, AS. bisceop, biscop, L. episcopus overseer, superintendent, bishop, fr. Gr. �, � over + � inspector, fr. root of �, �, to look to, perh. akin to L. specere to look at. See Spy, and cf. Episcopal.]

senses.d: To admit into the church by confirmation; to confirm; hence, to receive formally to favor.
To make seem younger, by operating on the teeth; as, to bishop an old horse or his teeth.

Bishop.etym: [From the name of the scoundrel who first practiced it. Youatt.]

senses.d: The part of a bridle, usually of iron, which is inserted in the mouth of a horse, and having appendages to which the reins are fastened.
q: The foamy bridle with the bit of gold. Chaucer.

senses.d: Fig.: Anything which curbs or restrains.

Bit.etym: [OE. bitt, bite, AS. bite, bite, fr. bītan to bite. See Bite, n. & v., and cf. Bit a morsel.]

senses.d: To put a bridle upon; to put the bit in the mouth of.
A part of anything, such as may be bitten off or taken into the mouth; a morsel; a bite. Hence: A small piece of anything; a little; a mite.
Somewhat; something, but not very great.
q: My young companion was a bit of a poet. T. Hook.

senses.d: A tool for boring, of various forms and sizes, usually turned by means of a brace or bitstock. See Bitstock.
The part of a key which enters the lock and acts upon the bolt and tumblers.
The cutting iron of a plane.
In the Southern and Southwestern States, a small silver coin (as the real) formerly current; commonly, one worth about 12 1/2 cents; also, the sum of 12 1/2 cents.

Bit.etym: [OE. bite, AS. bita, fr. bītan to bite; akin to D. beet, G. bissen bit, morsel, Icel. biti. See Bite, v., and cf. Bit part of a bridle.]

senses.d: In the British West Indies, a fourpenny piece, or groat.
To seize with the teeth, so that they enter or nip the thing seized; to lacerate, crush, or wound with the teeth; as, to bite an apple; to bite a crust; the dog bit a man.
q: Such smiling rogues as these, Like rats, oft bite the holy cords atwain. Shak.

senses.d: To puncture, abrade, or sting with an organ (of some insects) used in taking food.
To cause sharp pain, or smarting, to; to hurt or injure, in a literal or a figurative sense; as, pepper bites the mouth.
To cheat; to trick; to take in.
To take hold of; to hold fast; to adhere to; as, the anchor bites the ground.
q: The last screw of the rack having been turned so often that its purchase crumbled, . . . it turned and turned with nothing to bite. Dickens.

Bite.etym: [OE. biten, AS. bītan; akin to D. bijten, OS. bītan, OHG. bīzan, G. beissen, Goth. beitan, Icel. bīta, Sw. bita, Dan. bide, L. findere to cleave, Skr. bhid to cleave. √87. Cf. Fissure.]

senses.d: To seize something forcibly with the teeth; to wound with the teeth; to have the habit of so doing; as, does the dog bite?
To cause a smarting sensation; to have a property which causes such a sensation; to be pungent; as, it bites like pepper or mustard.
To cause sharp pain; to produce anguish; to hurt or injure; to have the property of so doing.
q: At the last it biteth like serpent, and stingeth like an adder. Prov. xxiii. 32.

senses.d: To take a bait into the mouth, as a fish does; hence, to take a tempting offer.
To take or keep a firm hold; as, the anchor bites.
The act of seizing with the teeth or mouth; the act of wounding or separating with the teeth or mouth; a seizure with the teeth or mouth, as of a bait; as, to give anything a hard bite.
q: I have known a very good fisher angle diligently four or six hours for a river carp, and not have a bite. Walton.

senses.d: The act of puncturing or abrading with an organ for taking food, as is done by some insects.
The wound made by biting; as, the pain of a dog's or snake's bite; the bite of a mosquito.
A morsel; as much as is taken at once by biting.
The hold which the short end of a lever has upon the thing to be lifted, or the hold which one part of a machine has upon another.
A cheat; a trick; a fraud.
q: The baser methods of getting money by fraud and bite, by deceiving and overreaching. Humorist.

senses.d: A sharper; one who cheats.
A blank on the edge or corner of a page, owing to a portion of the frisket, or something else, intervening between the type and paper.

Bite.etym: [OE. bite, bit, bitt, AS. bite bite, fr. bītan to bite, akin to Icel. bit, OS. biti, G. biss. See Bite, v., and cf. Bit.]

senses.d: To put round the bitts; as, to bitt the cable, in order to fasten it or to slacken it gradually, which is called veering away.
Terminating abruptly, as if bitten off; premorse.
AA turn of the cable which is round the bitts.
Having a peculiar, acrid, biting taste, like that of wormwood or an infusion of hops; as, a bitter medicine; bitter as aloes.
Causing pain or smart; piercing; painful; sharp; severe; as, a bitter cold day.
Causing, or fitted to cause, pain or distress to the mind; calamitous; poignant.
q: It is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God. Jer. ii. 19.

senses.d: Characterized by sharpness, severity, or cruelty; harsh; stern; virulent; as, bitter reproach.
q: Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them. Col. iii. 19.

senses.d: Mournful; sad; distressing; painful; pitiable.
q: The Egyptians . . . made their lives bitter with hard bondage. Ex. i. 14.

Bitter.syn: Acrid; sharp; harsh; pungent; stinging; cutting; severe; acrimonious.
Bitter.etym: [AS. biter; akin to Goth. baitrs, Icel. bitr, Dan., Sw., D., & G. bitter, OS. bittar, fr. root of E. bite. See Bite, v. t.]

senses.d: Any substance that is bitter. See Bitters.
To make bitter.
In a bitter manner.
A wading bird of the genus Botaurus, allied to the herons, of various species.

Bittern.etym: [OE. bitoure, betore, bitter, fr. F. butor; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: The brine which remains in salt works after the salt is concreted, having a bitter taste from the chloride of magnesium which it contains.
A very bitter compound of quassia, cocculus Indicus, etc., used by fraudulent brewers in adulterating beer.

The quality or state of being bitter, sharp, or acrid, in either a literal or figurative sense; implacableness; resentfulness; severity; keenness of reproach or sarcasm; deep distress, grief, or vexation of mind.
q: The lip that curls with bitterness. Percival.
I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. Job vii. 11.

senses.d: A state of extreme impiety or enmity to God.
q: Thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity. Acts viii. 23.

senses.d: Dangerous error, or schism, tending to draw persons to apostasy.
q: Looking diligently, . . . lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you. Heb. xii. 15.

senses.d: Destitute of light, or incapable of reflecting it; of the color of soot or coal; of the darkest or a very dark color, the opposite of white; characterized by such a color; as, black cloth; black hair or eyes.
q: O night, with hue so black! Shak.

senses.d: In a less literal sense: Enveloped or shrouded in darkness; very dark or gloomy; as, a black night; the heavens black with clouds.
q: I spy a black, suspicious, threatening cloud. Shak.

senses.d: Fig.: Dismal, gloomy, or forbidding, like darkness; destitute of moral light or goodness; atrociously wicked; cruel; mournful; calamitous; horrible.
Expressing menace, or discontent; threatening; sullen; foreboding; as, to regard one with black looks.

Black.syn: Dark; murky; pitchy; inky; somber; dusky; gloomy; swart; Cimmerian; ebon; atrocious.
Black.etym: [OE. blak, AS. blæc; akin to Icel. blakkr dark, swarthy, Sw. bläck ink, Dan. blæk, OHG. blach, LG. & D. blaken to burn with a black smoke. Not akin to AS. blāc, E. bleak pallid. �98.]

senses.d: Sullenly; threateningly; maliciously; so as to produce blackness.
That which is destitute of light or whiteness; the darkest color, or rather a destitution of all color; as, a cloth has a good black.
q: Black is the badge of hell, The hue of dungeons, and the suit of night. Shak.

senses.d: A black pigment or dye.
A negro; a person whose skin is of a black color, or shaded with black; esp. a member or descendant of certain African races.
A black garment or dress; as, she wears black
q: Friends weeping, and blacks, and obsequies, and the like show death terrible. Bacon.
That was the full time they used to wear blacks for the death of their fathers. Sir T. North.

senses.d: The part of a thing which is distinguished from the rest by being black.
q: The black or sight of the eye. Sir K. Digby.

senses.d: A stain; a spot; a smooch.
q: Defiling her white lawn of chastity with ugly blacks of lust. Rowley.

senses.d: To make black; to blacken; to soil; to sully.
q: They have their teeth blacked, both men and women, for they say a dog hath his teeth white, therefore they will black theirs. Hakluyt.
Sins which black thy soul. J. Fletcher.

senses.d: To make black and shining, as boots or a stove, by applying blacking and then polishing with a brush.
Somewhat black.
The quality or state of being black; black color; atrociousness or enormity in wickedness.
q: They're darker now than blackness. Donne.

senses.d: Properly, the leaf, or flat part of the leaf, of any plant, especially of gramineous plants. The term is sometimes applied to the spire of grasses.
q: The crimson dulse . . . with its waving blade. Percival.
First the blade, then ear, after that the full corn in the ear. Mark iv. 28.

senses.d: The cutting part of an instrument; as, the blade of a knife or a sword.
The broad part of an oar; also, one of the projecting arms of a screw propeller.
The scapula or shoulder blade.
The principal rafters of a roof.
The four large shell plates on the sides, and the five large ones of the middle, of the carapace of the sea turtle, which yield the best tortoise shell.
A sharp-witted, dashing, wild, or reckless, fellow; — a word of somewhat indefinite meaning.
q: He saw a turnkey in a trice Fetter a troublesome blade. Coleridge.

Blade.etym: [OE. blade, blad, AS. blæd leaf; akin to OS., D., Dan., & Sw. blad, Icel. blað, OHG. blat, G. blatt, and perh. to L. folium, Gr. φύλλον. The root is prob. the same as that of AS. blōwan, E. blow, to blossom. See Blow to blossom, and cf. Foil leaf of metal.]

senses.d: To furnish with a blade.
To put forth or have a blade.
q: As sweet a plant, as fair a flower, is faded As ever in the Muses' garden bladed. P. Fletcher.

senses.d: The flat part of the tongue immediately behind the tip, or point.
q: “Lower blade” implies, of course, the lower instead of the upper surface of the tongue.

senses.d: An inflammatory swelling or sore; a bulla, pustule, or blister.
q: Blotches and blains must all his flesh emboss. Milton.

senses.d: A bladder growing on the root of the tongue of a horse, against the windpipe, and stopping the breath.

Blain.etym: [OE. blein, bleyn, AS. blēgen; akin to Dan. blegn, D. blein; perh. fr. the same root as E. bladder. See Bladder.]

senses.d: To censure; to express disapprobation of; to find fault with; to reproach.
q: We have none to blame but ourselves. Tillotson.

senses.d: To bring reproach upon; to blemish.
q: She . . . blamed her noble blood. Spenser.
You were to blame, I must be plain with you. Shak.

Blame.etym: [OE. blamen, F. blâmer, OF. blasmer, fr. L. blasphemare to blaspheme, LL. also to blame, fr. Gr. βλασφημει̑ν to speak ill, to slander, to blaspheme, fr. βλάσφημοσ evil speaking, perh, for βλαψίφημοσ; βλάψισ injury (fr. βλάπτειν to injure) + φήμη a saying, fr. φάναι to say. Cf. Blaspheme, and see Fam

senses.d: An expression of disapprobation fir something deemed to be wrong; imputation of fault; censure.
q: Let me bear the blame forever. Gen. xiiii. 9.

senses.d: That which is deserving of censure or disapprobation; culpability; fault; crime; sin.
q: Holy and without blame before him in love. Eph. i. 4.

senses.d: Hurt; injury.

Blame.syn: Censure; reprehension; condemnation; reproach; fault; sin; crime; wrongdoing.
Blame.etym: [OE. blame, fr. F. blâme, OF. blasme, fr. blâmer, OF. blasmer, to blame. See Blame, v.]

senses.d: Free from blame; without fault; innocent; guiltless; — sometimes followed by of.
q: A bishop then must be blameless. 1 Tim. iii. 2.
Blameless still of arts that polish to deprave. Mallet.
We will be blameless of this thine oath. Josh. ii. 17.

senses.d: To speak of, or address, with impious irreverence; to revile impiously (anything sacred); as, to blaspheme the Holy Spirit.
q: So Dagon shall be magnified, and God, Besides whom is no god, compared with idols, Disglorified, blasphemed, and had in scorn. Milton.
How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge thyself on all those who thus continually blaspheme thy great and all-glorious name? Dr. W. Beveridge.

senses.d: Figuratively, of persons and things not religiously sacred, but held in high honor: To calumniate; to revile; to abuse.
q: You do blaspheme the good in mocking me. Shak.
Those who from our labors heap their board, Blaspheme their feeder and forget their lord. Pope.

Blaspheme.etym: [OE. blasfemēn, L. blasphemare, fr. Gr. βλασφημει̑ν: cf. F. blasphémer. See Blame, v.]

senses.d: To utter blasphemy.
q: He that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness. Mark iii. 29.

senses.d: One who blasphemes.
q: And each blasphemer quite escape the rod, Because the insult's not on man, but God ? Pope.

senses.d: Speaking or writing blasphemy; uttering or exhibiting anything impiously irreverent; profane; as, a blasphemous person; containing blasphemy; as, a blasphemous book; a blasphemous caricature.
q: Nor from the Holy One of Heaven Refrained his tongue blasphemous. Milton.

senses.d: In a blasphemous manner.

An indignity offered to God in words, writing, or signs; impiously irreverent words or signs addressed to, or used in reference to, God; speaking evil of God; also, the act of claiming the attributes or prerogatives of deity.
Figuratively, of things held in high honor: Calumny; abuse; vilification.
q: Punished for his blasphemy against learning. Bacon.

senses.d: A violent gust of wind.
q: And see where surly Winter passes off, Far to the north, and calls his ruffian blasts; His blasts obey, and quit the howling hill. Thomson.

senses.d: A forcible stream of air from an orifice, as from a bellows, the mouth, etc. Hence: The continuous blowing to which one charge of ore or metal is subjected in a furnace; as, to melt so many tons of iron at a blast.
The exhaust steam from and engine, driving a column of air out of a boiler chimney, and thus creating an intense draught through the fire; also, any draught produced by the blast.
The sound made by blowing a wind instrument; strictly, the sound produces at one breath.
q: One blast upon his bugle horn Were worth a thousand men. Sir W. Scott.
The blast of triumph o'er thy grave. Bryant.

senses.d: A sudden, pernicious effect, as if by a noxious wind, especially on animals and plants; a blight.
q: By the blast of God they perish. Job iv. 9.
Virtue preserved from fell destruction's blast. Shak.

senses.d: The act of rending, or attempting to rend, heavy masses of rock, earth, etc., by the explosion of gunpowder, dynamite, etc.; also, the charge used for this purpose.
A flatulent disease of sheep.

Blast.etym: [AS. blǣst a puff of wind, a blowing; akin to Icel. blāstr, OHG. blāst, and fr. a verb akin to Icel. blāsa to blow, OHG. blâsan, Goth. blēsan (in comp.); all prob. from the same root as E. blow. See Blow to eject air.]

senses.d: To injure, as by a noxious wind; to cause to wither; to stop or check the growth of, and prevent from fruit-bearing, by some pernicious influence; to blight; to shrivel.
q: Seven thin ears, and blasted with the east wind. Gen. xii. 6.

senses.d: Hence, to affect with some sudden violence, plague, calamity, or blighting influence, which destroys or causes to fail; to visit with a curse; to curse; to ruin; as, to blast pride, hopes, or character.
q: I'll cross it, though it blast me. Shak.
Blasted with excess of light. T. Gray.

senses.d: To confound by a loud blast or din.
q: Trumpeters, With brazen din blast you the city's ear. Shak.

senses.d: To rend open by any explosive agent, as gunpowder, dynamite, etc.; to shatter; as, to blast rocks.
To be blighted or withered; as, the bud blasted in the blossom.
To blow; to blow on a trumpet.
q: Toke his blake trumpe faste And gan to puffen and to blaste. Chaucer.

senses.d: Blighted; withered.
q: Upon this blasted heath.

senses.d: Confounded; accursed; detestable.
q: Some of her own blasted gypsies. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Rent open by an explosive.
q: The blasted quarry thunders, heard remote. Wordsworth.

senses.d: A blast; destruction by a blast, or by some pernicious cause.
q: I have smitten you with blasting and mildew. Amos iv. 9.

senses.d: The act or process of one who, or that which, blasts; the business of one who blasts.
A stream of gas or vapor emitting light and heat in the process of combustion; a bright flame.
Intense, direct light accompanied with heat; as, to seek shelter from the blaze of the sun.
q: O dark, dark, dark, amid the blaze of noon! Milton.

senses.d: A bursting out, or active display of any quality; an outburst; a brilliant display.
q: For what is glory but the blaze of fame? Milton.

senses.d: A white spot on the forehead of a horse.
A spot made on trees by chipping off a piece of the bark, usually as a surveyor's mark.
q: Three blazes in a perpendicular line on the same tree indicating a legislative road, the single blaze a settlement or neighborhood road. Carlton.

Blaze.etym: [OE. blase, AS. blæse, blase; akin to OHG. blass whitish, G. blass pale, MHG. blas torch, Icel. blys torch; perh. fr. the same root as E. blast. Cf. Blast, Blush, Blink.]

senses.d: To shine with flame; to glow with flame; as, the fire blazes.
To send forth or reflect glowing or brilliant light; to show a blaze.
q: And far and wide the icy summit blazed. Wordsworth.

senses.d: To be resplendent.
To mark (a tree) by chipping off a piece of the bark.
q: I found my way by the blazed trees. Hoffman.

senses.d: To designate by blazing; to mark out, as by blazed trees; as, to blaze a line or path.
q: Champollion died in 1832, having done little more than blaze out the road to be traveled by others. Nott.

senses.d: To make public far and wide; to make known; to render conspicuous.
q: On charitable lists he blazed his name. Pollok.
To blaze those virtues which the good would hide. Pope.

senses.d: To blazon.

Blaze.etym: [OE. blasen to blow; perh. confused with blast and blaze a flame, OE. blase. Cf. Blaze, v. i., and see Blast.]

senses.d: To make the noise of, or one like that of, a sheep; to cry like a sheep or calf.
q: Then suddenly was heard along the main, To low the ox, to bleat the woolly train. Pope
The ewe that will not hear her lamb when it baas, will never answer a calf when he bleats. Shak.

Bleat.etym: [OE. bleten, AS. bl�tan; akin to D. blaten, bleeten, OHG. blāzan, plāzan; prob. of imitative origin.]

senses.d: A plaintive cry of, or like that of, a sheep.
q: The bleat of fleecy sheep. Chapman's Homer.

senses.d: Crying as a sheep does.
q: Then came the shepherd back with his bleating flocks from the seaside. Longfellow.

senses.d: The cry of, or as of, a sheep.
To mark with deformity; to injure or impair, as anything which is well formed, or excellent; to mar, or make defective, either the body or mind.
q: Sin is a soil which blemisheth the beauty of thy soul. Brathwait.

senses.d: To tarnish, as reputation or character; to defame.
q: There had nothing passed between us that might blemish reputation. Oldys.

Blemish.etym: [OE. blemissen, blemishen, OF. blemir, blesmir, to strike, injure, soil, F. blêmir to grow pale, fr. OF. bleme, blesme, pale, wan, F. blême, prob. fr. Icel blāman the livid color of a wound, fr. blār blue; akin to E. blue. OF. blemir properly signifies to beat one (black and) blue, and to render blu

senses.d: Any mark of deformity or injury, whether physical or moral; anything that diminishes beauty, or renders imperfect that which is otherwise well formed; that which impairs reputation.
q: He shall take two he lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb of the first year without blemish. Lev. xiv. 10.
The reliefs of an envious man are those little blemishes and imperfections that discover themselves in an illustrious character. Spectator.

Blemish.syn: Spot; speck; flaw; deformity; stain; defect; fault; taint; reproach; dishonor; imputation; disgrace.

senses.d: To make or pronounce holy; to consecrate
q: And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it. Gen. ii. 3.

senses.d: To make happy, blithesome, or joyous; to confer prosperity or happiness upon; to grant divine favor to.
q: The quality of mercy is . . . twice blest; It blesseth him that gives and him that takes. Shak.
It hath pleased thee to bless the house of thy servant, that it may continue forever before thee. 1 Chron. xvii. 27 (R. V. )

senses.d: To express a wish or prayer for the happiness of; to invoke a blessing upon; — applied to persons.
q: Bless them which persecute you. Rom. xii. 14.

senses.d: To invoke or confer beneficial attributes or qualities upon; to invoke or confer a blessing on, — as on food.
q: Then he took the five loaves and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them. Luke ix. 16.

senses.d: To make the sign of the cross upon; to cross (one's self).
To guard; to keep; to protect.
To praise, or glorify; to extol for excellences.
q: Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Ps. ciii. 1.

senses.d: To esteem or account happy; to felicitate.
q: The nations shall bless themselves in him. Jer. iv. 3.

senses.d: To wave; to brandish.
q: And burning blades about their heads do bless. Spenser.
Round his armed head his trenchant blade he blest. Fairfax.

Bless.etym: [OE. blessien, bletsen, AS. bletsian, bledsian, bloedsian, fr. bl�d blood; prob. originally to consecrate by sprinkling with blood. See Blood.]

senses.d: Hallowed; consecrated; worthy of blessing or adoration; heavenly; holy.
q: O, run; prevent them with thy humble ode, And lay it lowly at his blessed feet. Milton.

senses.d: Enjoying happiness or bliss; favored with blessings; happy; highly favored.
q: All generations shall call me blessed. Luke i. 48.
Towards England's blessed shore. Shak.

senses.d: Imparting happiness or bliss; fraught with happiness; blissful; joyful.
Enjoying, or pertaining to, spiritual happiness, or heavenly felicity; as, the blessed in heaven.
q: Reverenced like a blessed saint. Shak.
Cast out from God and blessed vision. Milton.

senses.d: Beatified.
Used euphemistically, ironically, or intensively.
q: Not a blessed man came to set her free. R. D. Blackmore.

senses.d: The state of being blessed; happiness; felicity; bliss; heavenly joys; the favor of God.
q: The assurance of a future blessedness. Tillotson.

senses.d: The act of one who blesses.
A declaration of divine favor, or an invocation imploring divine favor on some or something; a benediction; a wish of happiness pronounces.
q: This is the blessing, where with Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel. Deut. xxxiii. 1.

senses.d: A means of happiness; that which promotes prosperity and welfare; a beneficent gift.
q: Nature's full blessings would be well dispensed. Milton.

senses.d: A gift.
Grateful praise or worship.
Destitute of the sense of seeing, either by natural defect or by deprivation; without sight.
q: He that is strucken blind can not forget The precious treasure of his eyesight lost. Shak.

senses.d: Not having the faculty of discernment; destitute of intellectual light; unable or unwilling to understand or judge; as, authors are blind to their own defects.
q: But hard be hardened, blind be blinded more, That they may stumble on, and deeper fall. Milton.

senses.d: Undiscerning; undiscriminating; inconsiderate.
q: This plan is recommended neither to blind approbation nor to blind reprobation. Jay.

senses.d: Having such a state or condition as a thing would have to a person who is blind; not well marked or easily discernible; hidden; unseen; concealed; as, a blind path; a blind ditch.
Involved; intricate; not easily followed or traced.
q: The blind mazes of this tangled wood. Milton.

senses.d: Having no openings for light or passage; as, a blind wall; open only at one end; as, a blind alley; a blind gut.
Unintelligible, or not easily intelligible; as, a blind passage in a book; illegible; as, blind writing.
Abortive; failing to produce flowers or fruit; as, blind buds; blind flowers.

Blind.etym: [AS.; akin to D., G., OS., Sw., & Dan. blind, Icel. blindr, Goth. blinds; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To make blind; to deprive of sight or discernment.
q: A blind guide is certainly a great mischief; but a guide that blinds those whom he should lead is . . . a much greater. South.

senses.d: To deprive partially of vision; to make vision difficult for and painful to; to dazzle.
q: Her beauty all the rest did blind. P. Fletcher.

senses.d: To darken; to obscure to the eye or understanding; to conceal; to deceive.
q: Such darkness blinds the sky. Dryden.
The state of the controversy between us he endeavored, with all his art, to blind and confound. Stillingfleet.

senses.d: To cover with a thin coating of sand and fine gravel; as a road newly paved, in order that the joints between the stones may be filled.
Something to hinder sight or keep out light; a screen; a cover; esp. a hinged screen or shutter for a window; a blinder for a horse.
Something to mislead the eye or the understanding, or to conceal some covert deed or design; a subterfuge.
A blindage. See Blindage.
A halting place.
To cover the eyes of, as with a bandage; to hinder from seeing.
q: And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face. Luke xxii. 64.

Blindfold.etym: [OE. blindfolden, blindfelden, blindfellen; AS. blind blind + prob. fellan, fyllan, to fell, strike down.]

senses.d: Having the eyes covered; blinded; having the mental eye darkened. Hence: Heedless; reckless; as, blindfold zeal; blindfold fury.
q: Fate's blindfold reign the atheist loudly owns. Dryden.

senses.d: State or condition of being blind, literally or figuratively.
The fluid which circulates in the principal vascular system of animals, carrying nourishment to all parts of the body, and bringing away waste products to be excreted. See under Arterial.
Relationship by descent from a common ancestor; consanguinity; kinship.
q: To share the blood of Saxon royalty. Sir W. Scott.
A friend of our own blood. Waller.

senses.d: Descent; lineage; especially, honorable birth; the highest royal lineage.
q: Give us a prince of blood, a son of Priam. Shak.
I am a gentleman of blood and breeding. Shak.

senses.d: Descent from parents of recognized breed; excellence or purity of breed.
The fleshy nature of man.
q: Nor gives it satisfaction to our blood. Shak.

senses.d: The shedding of blood; the taking of life, murder; manslaughter; destruction.
q: So wills the fierce, avenging sprite, Till blood for blood atones. Hood.

senses.d: A bloodthirsty or murderous disposition.
q: He was a thing of blood, whose every motion Was timed with dying cries. Shak.

senses.d: Temper of mind; disposition; state of the passions; — as if the blood were the seat of emotions.
q: When you perceive his blood inclined to mirth. Shak.

senses.d: A man of fire or spirit; a fiery spark; a gay, showy man; a rake.
q: Seest thou not . . . how giddily 'a turns about all the hot bloods between fourteen and five and thirty? Shak.
It was the morning costume of a dandy or blood. Thackeray.

senses.d: The juice of anything, especially if red.
q: He washed . . . his clothes in the blood of grapes. Gen. xiix. 11.

Blood.etym: [OE. blod, blood, AS. blōd; akin to D. bloed, OHG. bluot, G. blut, Goth. blōþ, Icel. blōð, Sw. & Dan. blod; prob. fr. the same root as E. blow to bloom. See Blow to bloom.]

senses.d: To bleed.
To stain, smear or wet, with blood.
q: Reach out their spears afar, And blood their points. Dryden.

senses.d: To give (hounds or soldiers) a first taste or sight of blood, as in hunting or war.
q: It was most important too that his troops should be blooded. Macaulay.

senses.d: To heat the blood of; to exasperate.
q: The auxiliary forces of the French and English were much blooded one against another. Bacon.

senses.d: Guilty of murder or bloodshed.
Eager to shed blood; cruel; sanguinary; murderous.
