Breach.syn: Rent; cleft; chasm; rift; aperture; gap; break; disruption; fracture; rupture; infraction; infringement; violation; quarrel; dispute; contention; difference; misunderstanding.
Breach.etym: [OE. breke, breche, AS. brice, gebrice, gebrece (in comp.), fr. brecan to break; akin to Dan. bræk, MHG. breche, gap, breach. See Break, and cf. Brake (the instrument), Brack a break]

senses.d: To make a breach or opening in; as, to breach the walls of a city.
To break the water, as by leaping out; — said of a whale.
To spread.

Bread.etym: [AS. brǣdan to make broad, to spread. See Broad, a.]

senses.d: An article of food made from flour or meal by moistening, kneading, and baking.
Food; sustenance; support of life, in general.
q: Give us this day our daily bread. Matt. vi. 11

Bread.etym: [AS. breád; akin to OFries. brād, OS. brōd, D. brood, G. brod, brot, Icel. brauð, Sw. & Dan. bröd. The root is probably that of E. brew. √93. See Brew.]

senses.d: To cover with bread crumbs, preparatory to cooking; as, breaded cutlets.
Distance from side to side of any surface or thing; measure across, or at right angles to the length; width.
q: Breadth of coloring is a prominent character in the painting of all great masters. Weale.

Breadth.etym: [OE. brede, breede, whence later bredette, AS. brǣdu, fr. brād broad. See Broad, a.]

senses.d: To strain apart; to sever by fracture; to divide with violence; as, to break a rope or chain; to break a seal; to break an axle; to break rocks or coal; to break a lock.
To lay open as by breaking; to divide; as, to break a package of goods.
To lay open, as a purpose; to disclose, divulge, or communicate.
q: Katharine, break thy mind to me. Shak.

senses.d: To infringe or violate, as an obligation, law, or promise.
q: Out, out, hyena! these are thy wonted arts . . . To break all faith, all vows, deceive, betray. Milton

senses.d: To interrupt; to destroy the continuity of; to dissolve or terminate; as, to break silence; to break one's sleep; to break one's journey.
q: Go, release them, Ariel; My charms I'll break, their senses I'll restore.

senses.d: To destroy the completeness of; to remove a part from; as, to break a set.
To destroy the arrangement of; to throw into disorder; to pierce; as, the cavalry were not able to break the British squares.
To shatter to pieces; to reduce to fragments.
q: The victim broke in pieces the musical instruments with which he had solaced the hours of captivity. Prescott.

senses.d: To exchange for other money or currency of smaller denomination; as, to break a five dollar bill.
To destroy the strength, firmness, or consistency of; as, to break flax.
To weaken or impair, as health, spirit, or mind.
q: An old man, broken with the storms of state. Shak.

senses.d: To diminish the force of; to lessen the shock of, as a fall or blow.
q: I'll rather leap down first, and break your fall. Dryden.

Break.syn: To dispart; rend; tear; shatter; batter; violate; infringe; demolish; destroy; burst; dislocate.
Break.etym: [OE. breken, AS. brecan; akin to OS. brekan, D. breken, OHG. brehhan, G. brechen, Icel. braka to creak, Sw. braka, bräkka to crack, Dan. brække to break, Goth. brikan to break, L. frangere. Cf. Bray to pound, Breach, Fragile.]

senses.d: To come apart or divide into two or more pieces, usually with suddenness and violence; to part; to burst asunder.
To open spontaneously, or by pressure from within, as a bubble, a tumor, a seed vessel, a bag.
q: Else the bottle break, and the wine runneth out. Math. ix. 17.

senses.d: To burst forth; to make its way; to come to view; to appear; to dawn.
q: The day begins to break, and night is fled. Shak.
And from the turf a fountain broke, and gurgled at our feet. Wordsworth.

senses.d: To burst forth violently, as a storm.
q: The clouds are still above; and, while I speak, A second deluge o'er our head may break. Dryden.

senses.d: To open up; to be scattered; to be dissipated; as, the clouds are breaking.
q: At length the darkness begins to break. Macaulay.

senses.d: To become weakened in constitution or faculties; to lose health or strength.
q: See how the dean begins to break; Poor gentleman! he droops apace. Swift.

senses.d: To be crushed, or overwhelmed with sorrow or grief; as, my heart is breaking.
To fall in business; to become bankrupt.
q: He that puts all upon adventures doth oftentimes break, and come to poverty. Bacn.

senses.d: To make an abrupt or sudden change; to change the gait; as, to break into a run or gallop.

To fail in musical quality; as, a singer's voice breaks when it is strained beyond its compass and a tone or note is not completed, but degenerates into an unmusical sound instead. Also, to change in tone, as a boy's voice at puberty.
To fall out; to terminate friendship.
q: To break upon the score of danger or expense is to be mean and narrow-spirited. Collier.
Fear me not, man; I will not break away. Shak.

senses.d: An opening made by fracture or disruption.
An interruption of continuity; change of direction; as, a break in a wall; a break in the deck of a ship.
An interruption; a pause; as, a break in friendship; a break in the conversation.
An interruption in continuity in writing or printing, as where there is an omission, an unfilled line, etc.
q: All modern trash is Set forth with numerous breaks and dashes. Swift.

senses.d: The first appearing, as of light in the morning; the dawn; as, the break of day; the break of dawn.
A large four-wheeled carriage, having a straight body and calash top, with the driver's seat in front and the footman's behind.
A device for checking motion, or for measuring friction. See Brake, n. 9 & 10.

Break.etym: [See Break, v. t., and cf. Brake (the instrument), Breach, Brack a crack.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, breaks.
q: I'll be no breaker of the law. Shak.

senses.d: Specifically: A machine for breaking rocks, or for breaking coal at the mines; also, the building in which such a machine is placed.
A small water cask.
A wave breaking into foam against the shore, or against a sand bank, or a rock or reef near the surface.
q: The breakers were right beneath her bows. Longfellow.

senses.d: The fore part of the body, between the neck and the belly; the chest; as, the breast of a man or of a horse.

Either one of the protuberant glands, situated on the front of the chest or thorax in the female of man and of some other mammalia, in which milk is secreted for the nourishment of the young; a mamma; a teat.
q: My brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother. Cant. viii. 1.

senses.d: Anything resembling the human breast, or bosom; the front or forward part of anything; as, a chimney breast; a plow breast; the breast of a hill.
q: Mountains on whose barren breast The laboring clouds do often rest. Milton.

senses.d: The face of a coal working.
The seat of consciousness; the repository of thought and self-consciousness, or of secrets; the seat of the affections and passions; the heart.
q: He has a loyal breast. Shak.

senses.d: The power of singing; a musical voice; — so called, probably, from the connection of the voice with the lungs, which lie within the breast.
q: By my troth, the fool has an excellent breast. Shak.

Breast.etym: [OE. brest, breost, As. breóst; akin to Icel. brjōst, Sw. bröst, Dan. bryst, Goth. brusts, OS. briost, D. borst, G. brust.]

senses.d: To meet, with the breast; to struggle with or oppose manfully; as, to breast the storm or waves.
q: The court breasted the popular current by sustaining the demurrer. Wirt.

senses.d: A plate of metal covering the breast as defensive armor.
q: Before his old rusty breastplate could be scoured, and his cracked headpiece mended. Swift.

senses.d: A piece against which the workman presses his breast in operating a breast drill, or other similar tool.
A strap that runs across a horse's breast.

A part of the vestment of the high priest, worn upon the front of the ephod. It was a double piece of richly embroidered stuff, a span square, set with twelve precious stones, on which were engraved the names of the twelve tribes of Israel. See Ephod.
The air inhaled and exhaled in respiration; air which, in the process of respiration, has parted with oxygen and has received carbonic acid, aqueous vapor, warmth, etc.
q: Melted as breath into the wind. Shak.

senses.d: The act of breathing naturally or freely; the power or capacity to breathe freely; as, I am out of breath.
The power of respiration, and hence, life.
q: Thou takest away their breath, they die. Ps. civ. 29.

senses.d: Time to breathe; respite; pause.
q: Give me some breath, some little pause. Shak.

senses.d: A single respiration, or the time of making it; a single act; an instant.
q: He smiles and he frowns in a breath. Dryden.

senses.d: Fig.: That which gives or strengthens life.
q: The earthquake voice of victory, To thee the breath of life. Byron.

senses.d: A single word; the slightest effort; a trifle.
q: A breath can make them, as a breath has made. Goldsmith.

senses.d: A very slight breeze; air in gentle motion.
q: Calm and unruffled as a summer's sea, when not a breath of wind flies o'er its surface. Addison.

senses.d: Fragrance; exhalation; odor; perfume.
q: The breath of flowers. Bacon.

senses.d: Gentle exercise, causing a quicker respiration.
q: An after dinner's breath. Shak.

Breath.etym: [OE. breth, breeth, AS. brǣð odor, scent, breath; cf. OHG. brādam steam, vapor, breath, G. brodem, and possibly E. Brawn, and Breed.]

senses.d: To respire; to inhale and exhale air; hence;, to live.
q: Breathes there a man with soul so dead? Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To take breath; to rest from action.
q: Well! breathe awhile, and then to it again! Shak.

senses.d: To pass like breath; noiselessly or gently; to exhale; to emanate; to blow gently.
q: The air breathes upon us here most sweetly. Shak.
There breathes a living fragrance from the shore. Byron.

senses.d: To inhale and exhale in the process of respiration; to respire.
q: To view the light of heaven, and breathe the vital air. Dryden.

senses.d: To inject by breathing; to infuse; — with into.
q: Able to breathe life into a stone. Shak.
And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Gen. ii. 7.

senses.d: To emit or utter by the breath; to utter softly; to whisper; as, to breathe a vow.
q: He softly breathed thy name. Dryden.
Or let the church, our mother, breathe her curse, A mother's curse, on her revolting son. Shak.

senses.d: To exhale; to emit, as breath; as, the flowers breathe odors or perfumes.
To express; to manifest; to give forth.
q: Others articles breathe the same severe spirit. Milner.

senses.d: To act upon by the breath; to cause to sound by breathing.
To promote free respiration in; to exercise.
q: And every man should beat thee. I think thou wast created for men to breathe themselves upon thee. Shak.

senses.d: To suffer to take breath, or recover the natural breathing; to rest; as, to breathe a horse.
q: A moment breathed his panting steed. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: To put out of breath; to exhaust.
q: Mr. Tulkinghorn arrives in his turret room, a little breathed by the journey up. Dickens.

senses.d: To utter without vocality, as the nonvocal consonants.
q: The same sound may be pronounces either breathed, voiced, or whispered. H. Sweet.
Breathed elements, being already voiceless, remain unchanged . H. Sweet.

senses.d: Respiration; the act of inhaling and exhaling air.
q: Subject to a difficulty of breathing. Melmoth.

senses.d: Air in gentle motion.
Any gentle influence or operation; inspiration; as, the breathings of the Spirit.
Aspiration; secret prayer.
Exercising; promotion of respiration.
q: Here is a lady that wants breathing too; And I have heard, you knights of Tyre Are excellent in making ladies trip. Shak.

senses.d: Utterance; communication or publicity by words.
q: I am sorry to give breathing to my purpose. Shak.

senses.d: Breathing place; vent.
Stop; pause; delay.
q: You shake the head at so long a breathing. Shak.

senses.d: Also, in a wider sense, the sound caused by the friction of the outgoing breath in the throat, mouth, etc., when the glottis is wide open; aspiration; the sound expressed by the letter h.
A mark to indicate aspiration or its absence. See Rough breathing, Smooth breathing, below.
The lower part of the body behind; the buttocks.
Breeches.
The hinder part of anything; esp., the part of a cannon, or other firearm, behind the chamber.
The external angle of knee timber, the inside of which is called the throat.
To put into, or clothe with, breeches.
q: A great man . . . anxious to know whether the blacksmith's youngest boy was breeched. Macaulay.

senses.d: To cover as with breeches.
q: Their daggers unmannerly breeched with gore. Shak.

senses.d: To fit or furnish with a breech; as, to breech a gun.
To whip on the breech.
q: Had not a courteous serving man conveyed me away, whilst he went to fetch whips, I think, in my conscience, he would have breeched me. Old Play.

senses.d: To fasten with breeching.
A garment worn by men, covering the hips and thighs; smallclothes.
q: His jacket was red, and his breeches were blue. Coleridge.

senses.d: Trousers; pantaloons.

Breeches.etym: [OE. brech, brek, AS. brēk, pl. of brōc breech, breeches; akin to Icel. brōk breeches, ODan. brog, D. broek, G. bruch; cf. L. bracae, braccae, which is of Celtic origin. Cf. Brail.]

senses.d: To produce as offspring; to bring forth; to bear; to procreate; to generate; to beget; to hatch.
q: Yet every mother breeds not sons alike. Shak.
If the sun breed maggots in a dead dog. Shak.

senses.d: To take care of in infancy, and through the age of youth; to bring up; to nurse and foster.
q: To bring thee forth with pain, with care to breed. Dryden.
Born and bred on the verge of the wilderness. Everett.

senses.d: To educate; to instruct; to form by education; to train; — sometimes followed by up.
q: But no care was taken to breed him a Protestant. Bp. Burnet.
His farm may not remove his children too far from him, or the trade he breeds them up in. Locke.

senses.d: To engender; to cause; to occasion; to originate; to produce; as, to breed a storm; to breed disease.
q: Lest the place And my quaint habits breed astonishment. Milton.

senses.d: To give birth to; to be the native place of; as, a pond breeds fish; a northern country breeds stout men.
To raise, as any kind of stock.
To produce or obtain by any natural process.
q: Children would breed their teeth with less danger. Locke.

Breed.syn: To engender; generate; beget; produce; hatch; originate; bring up; nourish; train; instruct.
Breed.etym: [OE. breden, AS. brēdan to nourish, cherish, keep warm, from brōd brood; akin to D. broeden to brood, OHG. bruoten, G. brüten. See Brood.]

senses.d: To bear and nourish young; to reproduce or multiply itself; to be pregnant.
q: That they breed abundantly in the earth. Gen. viii. 17.
The mother had never bred before. Carpenter.
Ant. Is your gold and silver ewes and rams? Shy. I can not tell. I make it breed as fast. Shak.

senses.d: To be formed in the parent or dam; to be generated, or to grow, as young before birth.
To have birth; to be produced or multiplied.
q: Heavens rain grace On that which breeds between them. Shak.

senses.d: To raise a breed; to get progeny.
q: The kind of animal which you wish to breed from. Gardner.

senses.d: A race or variety of men or other animals (or of plants), perpetuating its special or distinctive characteristics by inheritance.
q: Twice fifteen thousand hearts of England's breed. Shak.
Greyhounds of the best breed. Carpenter.

senses.d: Class; sort; kind; — of men, things, or qualities.
q: Are these the breed of wits so wondered at? Shak.
This courtesy is not of the right breed. Shak.

senses.d: A number produced at once; a brood.
The act or process of generating or bearing.
The raising or improving of any kind of domestic animals; as, farmers should pay attention to breeding.
Nurture; education; formation of manners.
q: She had her breeding at my father's charge. Shak.

senses.d: Deportment or behavior in the external offices and decorums of social life; manners; knowledge of, or training in, the ceremonies, or polite observances of society.
q: Delicacy of breeding, or that polite deference and respect which civility obliges us either to express or counterfeit towards the persons with whom we converse. Hume.

senses.d: Descent; pedigree; extraction.
q: Honest gentlemen, I know not your breeding. Shak.

Breeding.syn: Education; instruction; nurture; training; manners. See Education.

senses.d: A gift begged; a present.
A price, reward, gift, or favor bestowed or promised with a view to prevent the judgment or corrupt the conduct of a judge, witness, voter, or other person in a position of trust.
q: Undue reward for anything against justice is a bribe. Hobart.

senses.d: That which seduces; seduction; allurement.
q: Not the bribes of sordid wealth can seduce to leave these ever�blooming sweets. Akenside.

Bribe.etym: [F. bribe a lump of bread, scraps, leavings of meals (that are generally given to a beggar), LL. briba scrap of bread; cf. OF. briber, brifer, to eat gluttonously, to beg, and OHG. bilibi food.]

senses.d: To rob or steal.

To give or promise a reward or consideration to (a judge, juror, legislator, voter, or other person in a position of trust) with a view to prevent the judgment or corrupt the conduct; to induce or influence by a bribe; to give a bribe to.
q: Neither is he worthy who bribes a man to vote against his conscience. F. W. Robertson.

senses.d: To gain by a bribe; of induce as by a bribe.
To commit robbery or theft.
To give a bribe to a person; to pervert the judgment or corrupt the action of a person in a position of trust, by some gift or promise.
q: An attempt to bribe, though unsuccessful, has been holden to be criminal, and the offender may be indicted. Bouvier.
The bard may supplicate, but cannot bribe. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Robbery; extortion.
The act or practice of giving or taking bribes; the act of influencing the official or political action of another by corrupt inducements.

Bribery.etym: [OE. brybery rascality, OF. briberie. See Bribe, n.]

senses.d: A block or clay tempered with water, sand, etc., molded into a regular form, usually rectangular, and sun-dried, or burnt in a kiln, or in a heap or stack called a clamp.
q: The Assyrians appear to have made much less use of bricks baked in the furnace than the Babylonians. Layard.

senses.d: Bricks, collectively, as designating that kind of material; as, a load of brick; a thousand of brick.
q: Some of Palladio's finest examples are of brick. Weale.

senses.d: Any oblong rectangular mass; as, a brick of maple sugar; a penny brick (of bread).
A good fellow; a merry person; as, you 're a brick.

Brick.etym: [OE. brik, F. brique; of Ger. origin; cf. AS. brice a breaking, fragment, Prov. E. brique piece, brique de pain, equiv. to AS. hlāfes brice, fr. the root of E. break. See Break.]

senses.d: To lay or pave with bricks; to surround, line, or construct with bricks.
To imitate or counterfeit a brick wall on, as by smearing plaster with red ocher, making the joints with an edge tool, and pointing them.
A kiln, or furnace, in which bricks are baked or burnt; or a pile of green bricks, laid loose, with arches underneath to receive the wood or fuel for burning them.
A woman newly married, or about to be married.
q: Has by his own experience tried How much the wife is dearer than the bride. Lyttleton.
I will show thee the bride, the Lamb's wife. Rev. xxi. 9.

senses.d: Fig.: An object ardently loved.

Bride.etym: [OE. bride, brid, brude, brud, burd, AS. brȳd; akin to OFries. breid, OSax. brūd, D. bruid, OHG. prūt, brūt, G. braut, Icel. brūðr, Sw. & Dan. brud, Goth. brūþs; cf. Armor. pried spouse, W. priawd a married person.]

senses.d: To make a bride of.
The nuptial apartment.
A man newly married, or just about to be married.

Bridegroom.etym: [OE. bridegome, brudgume, AS. brȳdguma (akin to OS. brūdigumo, D. bruidegom, bruigom, OHG. prūtigomo, MHG. briutegome, G. bräutigam); AS. brȳd bride + guma man, akin to Goth. guma, Icel. gumi, OHG. gomo, L. homo; the insertion of r being caused by confusion with groom. See Bride, and cf. Groom, Homa

senses.d: The head gear with which a horse is governed and restrained, consisting of a headstall, a bit, and reins, with other appendages.
A restraint; a curb; a check.
The piece in the interior of a gun lock, which holds in place the tumbler, sear, etc.
A span of rope, line, or chain made fast as both ends, so that another rope, line, or chain may be attached to its middle.

Bridle.etym: [OE. bridel, AS. bridel; akin to OHG. britil, brittil, D. breidel, and possibly to E. braid. Cf. Bridoon.]

senses.d: To put a bridle upon; to equip with a bridle; as, to bridle a horse.
q: He bridled her mouth with a silkweed twist. Drake.

senses.d: To restrain, guide, or govern, with, or as with, a bridle; to check, curb, or control; as, to bridle the passions; to bridle a muse.
q: Savoy and Nice, the keys of Italy, and the citadel in her hands to bridle Switzerland, are in that consolidation. Burke.

Bridle.syn: To check; restrain; curb; govern; control; repress; master; subdue.

senses.d: To hold up the head, and draw in the chin, as an expression of pride, scorn, or resentment; to assume a lofty manner; — usually with up.
q: By her bridling up I perceived she expected to be treated hereafter not as Jenny Distaff, but Mrs. Tranquillus. Tatler.

senses.d: Short in duration.
q: How brief the life of man. Shak.

senses.d: Concise; terse; succinct.
q: The brief style is that which expresseth much in little. B. Jonson.

senses.d: Rife; common; prevalent.

Brief.syn: Short; concise; succinct; summary; compendious; condensed; terse; curt; transitory; short-lived.
Brief.etym: [OE. bref, F. brief, bref, fr. L. brevis; akin to Gr. � short, and perh. to Skr. barh to tear. Cf. Breve.]

senses.d: Briefly.
q: Adam, faltering long, thus answered brief. Milton.

senses.d: Soon; quickly.
A short concise writing or letter; a statement in few words.
q: Bear this sealed brief, With winged hastle, to the lord marshal. Shak.
And she told me In a sweet, verbal brief. Shak.

senses.d: An epitome.
q: Each woman is a brief of womankind. Overbury.

senses.d: An abridgment or concise statement of a client's case, made out for the instruction of counsel in a trial at law. This word is applied also to a statement of the heads or points of a law argument.
q: It was not without some reference to it that I perused many a brief. Sir J. Stephen.

senses.d: A writ; a breve. See Breve, n., 2.
A writ issuing from the chancery, directed to any judge ordinary, commanding and authorizing that judge to call a jury to inquire into the case, and upon their verdict to pronounce sentence.
A letter patent, from proper authority, authorizing a collection or charitable contribution of money in churches, for any public or private purpose.
To make an abstract or abridgment of; to shorten; as, to brief pleadings.
Concisely; in few words.
A plant with a slender woody stem bearing stout prickles; especially, species of Rosa, Rubus, and Smilax.
Fig.: Anything sharp or unpleasant to the feelings.
q: The thorns and briers of reproof. Cowper.

Brier.etym: [OE. brere, brer, AS. brēr, brær; cf. Ir. briar prickle, thorn, brier, pin, Gael. preas bush, brier, W. prys, prysg.]

senses.d: A coast of armor for the body, consisting of scales or plates, sometimes overlapping each other, generally of metal, and sewed to linen or other material. It was worn in the Middle Ages.
q: Then put on all thy gorgeous arms, thy helmet, And brigandine of brass. Milton.

Brigandine.etym: [F. brigandine (cf. It. brigantina), fr. OF. brigant. See Brigand.]

senses.d: Radiating or reflecting light; shedding or having much light; shining; luminous; not dark.
q: The sun was bright o'erhead. Longfellow.
The earth was dark, but the heavens were bright. Drake.
The public places were as bright as at noonday. Macaulay.

senses.d: Transmitting light; clear; transparent.
q: From the brightest wines He 'd turn abhorrent. Thomson.

senses.d: Having qualities that render conspicuous or attractive, or that affect the mind as light does the eye; resplendent with charms; as, bright beauty.
q: Bright as an angel new-dropped from the sky. Parnell.

senses.d: Having a clear, quick intellect; intelligent.
Sparkling with wit; lively; vivacious; shedding cheerfulness and joy around; cheerful; cheery.
q: Be bright and jovial among your guests. Shak.

senses.d: Illustrious; glorious.
q: In the brightest annals of a female reign. Cotton.

senses.d: Manifest to the mind, as light is to the eyes; clear; evident; plain.
q: That he may with more ease, with brighter evidence, and with surer success, draw the bearner on. I. Watts.

senses.d: Of brilliant color; of lively hue or appearance.
q: Here the bright crocus and blue violet grew. Pope.

Bright.syn: Shining; splending; luminous; lustrous; brilliant; resplendent; effulgent; refulgent; radiant; sparkling; glittering; lucid; beamy; clear; transparent; illustrious; witty; clear; vivacious; sunny.
Bright.etym: [OE. briht, AS. beorht, briht; akin to OS. berht, OHG. beraht, Icel. bjartr, Goth. baírhts. √94.]

senses.d: Splendor; brightness.
q: Dark with excessive bright thy skirts appear. Milton.

senses.d: Brightly.
q: I say it is the moon that shines so bright. Shak.

senses.d: The quality or state of being bright; splendor; luster; brilliancy; clearness.
q: A sudden brightness in his face appear. Crabbe.

senses.d: Acuteness (of the faculties); sharpness 9wit.
q: The brightness of his parts . . . distinguished him. Prior.

Brightness.syn: Splendor; luster; radiance; resplendence; brilliancy; effulgence; glory; clearness.

senses.d: The rim, border, or upper edge of a cup, dish, or any hollow vessel used for holding anything.
q: Saw I that insect on this goblet's brim I would remove it with an anxious pity. Coleridge.

senses.d: The edge or margin, as of a fountain, or of the water contained in it; the brink; border.
q: The feet of the priests that bare the ark were dipped in the brim of the water. Josh. iii. 15.

senses.d: The rim of a hat.

Brim.etym: [OE. brim, brimme, AS. brymme edge, border; akin to Icel. barmr, Sw. bräm, Dan. bræmme, G. brame, bräme. Possibly the same word as AS. brim surge, sea, and properly meaning, the line of surf at the border of the sea, and akin to L. fremere to roar, murmur. Cf. Breeze a fly.]

senses.d: To be full to the brim.
To fill to the brim, upper edge, or top.
q: Arrange the board and brim the glass. Tennyson.

senses.d: Fierce; sharp; cold. See Breme.
Sulphur; See Sulphur.

Brimstone.etym: [OE. brimston, bremston, bernston, brenston; cf. Icel. brennistein. See Burn, v. t., and Stone.]

senses.d: Made of, or pertaining to, brimstone; as, brimstone matches.
q: From his brimstone bed at break of day A-walking the devil has gone. Coleridge.

senses.d: To convey to the place where the speaker is or is to be; to bear from a more distant to a nearer place; to fetch.
q: And as she was going to fetch it, he called to her, and said, Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread. 1 Kings xvii. 11.
To France shall we convey you safe, And bring you back. Shak.

senses.d: To cause the accession or obtaining of; to procure; to make to come; to produce; to draw to.
q: There is nothing will bring you more honor . . . than to do what right in justice you may. Bacon.

senses.d: To convey; to move; to carry or conduct.
q: In distillation, the water . . . brings over with it some part of the oil of vitriol. Sir I. Newton.

senses.d: To persuade; to induce; to draw; to lead; to guide.
q: It seems so preposterous a thing . . . that they do not easily bring themselves to it. Locke.
The nature of the things . . . would not suffer him to think otherwise, how, or whensoever, he is brought to reflect on them. Locke.

senses.d: To produce in exchange; to sell for; to fetch; as, what does coal bring per ton?

Bring.syn: To fetch; bear; carry; convey; transport; import; procure; produce; cause; adduce; induce.
Bring.etym: [OE. bringen, AS. bringan; akin to OS. brengian, D. brengen, Fries. brenga, OHG. bringan, G. bringen, Goth. briggan.]

senses.d: One who brings.
q: Yet the first bringer of unwelcome news Hath but a losing office. Shak.

senses.d: The edge, margin, or border of a steep place, as of a precipice; a bank or edge, as of a river or pit; a verge; a border; as, the brink of a chasm. Also Fig.
q: The plashy brink of weedy lake. Bryant.

Brink.etym: [Dan. brink edge, verge; akin to Sw. brink declivity, hill, Icel. brekka; cf. LG. brink a grassy hill, W. bryn hill, bryncyn hillock.]

senses.d: Wide; extend in breadth, or from side to side; — opposed to narrow; as, a broad street, a broad table; an inch broad.
Extending far and wide; extensive; vast; as, the broad expanse of ocean.
Extended, in the sense of diffused; open; clear; full.

Fig.: Having a large measure of any thing or quality; not limited; not restrained; — applied to any subject, and retaining the literal idea more or less clearly, the precise meaning depending largely on the substantive.
q: A broad mixture of falsehood. Locke.

senses.d: Comprehensive; liberal; enlarged.
q: The words in the Constitution are broad enough to include the case. D. Daggett.
In a broad, statesmanlike, and masterly way. E. Everett.

senses.d: Plain; evident; as, a broad hint.
Free; unrestrained; unconfined.
q: As broad and general as the casing air. Shak.

senses.d: Characterized by breadth. See Breadth.
Cross; coarse; indelicate; as, a broad compliment; a broad joke; broad humor.
Strongly marked; as, a broad Scotch accent.
q: It is as broad as long, whether they rise to others, or bring others down to them. L'Estrange.

Broad.syn: Wide; large; ample; expanded; spacious; roomy; extensive; vast; comprehensive; liberal.
Broad.etym: [OE. brod, brad, AS. brād; akin to OS. brēd, D. breed, G. breit, Icel. brei�r, Sw. & Dan. bred, Goth. braids. Cf. Breadth.]

senses.d: The broad part of anything; as, the broad of an oar.
The spread of a river into a sheet of water; a flooded fen.
A lathe tool for turning down the insides and bottoms of cylinders.
To braid.
To embroider.
q: They shall make a broidered coat. Ex. xxviii. 4.

Broider.etym: [OE. broiden, brouden, F. broder, confused with E. braid; F. broder is either the same word as border to border (see Border), or perh. of Celtic origin; cf. W. brathu to sting, stab, Ir. & Gael. brod goad, prickle, OE. brod a goad; and also Icel. broddr a spike, a sting, AS. brord a point.]

senses.d: A tumult; a noisy quarrel; a disturbance; a brawl; contention; discord, either between individuals or in the state.
q: I will own that there is a haughtiness and fierceness in human nature which will which will cause innumerable broils, place men in what situation you please. Burke.

Broil.syn: Contention; fray; affray; tumult; altercation; dissension; discord; contest; conflict; brawl; uproar.
Broil.etym: [F. brouiller to disorder, from LL. brogilus, broilus, brolium, thicket, wood, park; of uncertain origin; cf. W. brog a swelling out, OHG. prōil marsh, G. brühl, MHG. brogen to rise. The meaning tumult, confusion, comes apparently from tangled undergrowth, thicket, and this possibly from the meaning

senses.d: To cook by direct exposure to heat over a fire, esp. upon a gridiron over coals.
To subject to great (commonly direct) heat.

Broil.etym: [OE. broilen, OF. bruillir, fr. bruir to broil, burn; of Ger. origin; cf. MHG. brüejen, G. brühen, to scald, akin to E. brood.]

senses.d: To be subjected to the action of heat, as meat over the fire; to be greatly heated, or to be made uncomfortable with heat.
q: The planets and comets had been broiling in the sun. Cheyne.

senses.d: Separated into parts or pieces by violence; divided into fragments; as, a broken chain or rope; a broken dish.
Disconnected; not continuous; also, rough; uneven; as, a broken surface.
Fractured; cracked; disunited; sundered; strained; apart; as, a broken reed; broken friendship.
Made infirm or weak, by disease, age, or hardships.
q: The one being who remembered him as he been before his mind was broken. G. Eliot.
The broken soldier, kindly bade to stay, Sat by his fire, and talked the night away. Goldsmith.

senses.d: Subdued; humbled; contrite.
q: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. Ps. li. 17.

senses.d: Subjugated; trained for use, as a horse.
Crushed and ruined as by something that destroys hope; blighted.
Not carried into effect; not adhered to; violated; as, a broken promise, vow, or contract; a broken law.
Ruined financially; incapable of redeeming promises made, or of paying debts incurred; as, a broken bank; a broken tradesman.
Imperfectly spoken, as by a foreigner; as, broken English; imperfectly spoken on account of emotion; as, to say a few broken words at parting.
q: Amidst the broken words and loud weeping of those grave senators. Macaulay.

senses.d: The young birds hatched at one time; a hatch; as, a brood of chickens.
q: As a hen doth gather her brood under her wings. Luke xiii. 34.
A hen followed by a brood of ducks. Spectator.

senses.d: The young from the same dam, whether produced at the same time or not; young children of the same mother, especially if nearly of the same age; offspring; progeny; as, a woman with a brood of children.
q: The lion roars and gluts his tawny brood. Wordsworth.

senses.d: That which is bred or produced; breed; species.
q: Flocks of the airy brood, (Cranes, geese or long-necked swans). Chapman.

senses.d: Heavy waste in tin and copper ores.

Brood.etym: [OE. brod, AS. brōd; akin to D. broed, OHG. bruot, G. brut, and also to G. brühe broth, MHG. brüeje, and perh. to E. brawn, breath. Cf. Breed, v. t.]

senses.d: Sitting or inclined to sit on eggs.
Kept for breeding from; as, a brood mare; brood stock; having young; as, a brood sow.

To sit on and cover eggs, as a fowl, for the purpose of warming them and hatching the young; or to sit over and cover young, as a hen her chickens, in order to warm and protect them; hence, to sit quietly, as if brooding.
q: Birds of calm sir brooding on the charmed wave. Milton.

senses.d: To have the mind dwell continuously or moodily on a subject; to think long and anxiously; to be in a state of gloomy, serious thought; — usually followed by over or on; as, to brood over misfortunes.
q: Brooding on unprofitable gold. Dryden.
Brooding over all these matters, the mother felt like one who has evoked a spirit. Hawthorne.
When with downcast eyes we muse and brood. Tennyson.

senses.d: To sit over, cover, and cherish; as, a hen broods her chickens.
To cherish with care.
To think anxiously or moodily upon.
q: You'll sit and brood your sorrows on a throne. Dryden.

senses.d: A natural stream of water smaller than a river or creek.
q: The Lord thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water. Deut. viii. 7.
Empires itself, as doth an inland brook Into the main of waters. Shak.

Brook.etym: [OE. brok, broke, brook, AS. brōc; akin to D. broek, LG. brōk, marshy ground, OHG. pruoh, G. bruch marsh; prob. fr. the root of E. break, so as that it signifies water breaking through the earth, a spring or brook, as well as a marsh. See Break, v. t.]

senses.d: To use; to enjoy.
To bear; to endure; to put up with; to tolerate; as, young men can not brook restraint.
q: Shall we, who could not brook one lord, Crouch to the wicked ten? Macaulay.

senses.d: To deserve; to earn.

Brook.etym: [OE. broken, bruken, to use, enjoy, digest, AS. br�can; akin to D. gebruiken to use, OHG. pr�hhan, G. brauchen, gebrauchen, Icel. br�ka, Goth. br�kjan, and L. frui, to enjoy. Cf. Fruit, Broker.]

senses.d: Liquid in which flesh (and sometimes other substances, as barley or rice) has been boiled; thin or simple soup.
q: I am sure by your unprejudiced discourses that you love broth better than soup. Addison.

Broth.etym: [AS. bro�; akin to OHG. brod, brot; cf. Ir. broth, Gael. brot. √93. Cf. Brewis, Brew.]

senses.d: A male person who has the same father and mother with another person, or who has one of them only. In the latter case he is more definitely called a half brother, or brother of the half blood.
q: Two of us in the churchyard lie, My sister and my brother. Wordsworth.

senses.d: One related or closely united to another by some common tie or interest, as of rank, profession, membership in a society, toil, suffering, etc.; — used among judges, clergymen, monks, physicians, lawyers, professors of religion, etc.
q: We few, we happy few, we band of brothers, For he to-day that sheds his blood with me Shall be my brother. Shak.

senses.d: One who, or that which, resembles another in distinctive qualities or traits of character.
q: He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster. Prov. xviii. 9.
That April morn Of this the very brother. Wordsworth.
For of whom such massacre Make they but of their brethren, men of men? Milton.

Brother.etym: [OE. brother, AS. brōðor; akin to OS. brothar, D. broeder, OHG. pruodar, G. bruder, Icel. brōðir, Sw. & Dan. broder, Goth. brōþar, Ir. brathair, W. brawd, pl. brodyr, Lith. brolis, Lett. brahlis, Russ. brat', Pol. & Serv. brat, OSlav. bratrŭ, L. frater, Skr. bhrātṛ, Zend bratar brother, Gr. φράτηρ,

senses.d: To make a brother of; to call or treat as a brother; to admit to a brotherhood.
The state of being brothers or a brother.
An association for any purpose, as a society of monks; a fraternity.
The whole body of persons engaged in the same business, — especially those of the same profession; as, the legal or medical brotherhood.
Persons, and, poetically, things, of a like kind.
q: A brotherhood of venerable trees. Wordsworth.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers; becoming to brothers; kind; affectionate; as, brotherly love.
Like a brother; affectionately; kindly.
The prominent ridge over the eye, with the hair that covers it, forming an arch above the orbit.
q: And his arched brow, pulled o'er his eyes, With solemn proof proclaims him wise. Churchill.

senses.d: The hair that covers the brow (ridge over the eyes); the eyebrow.
q: 'T is not your inky brows, your brack silk hair. Shak.

senses.d: The forehead; as, a feverish brow.
q: Beads of sweat have stood upon thy brow. Shak.

senses.d: The general air of the countenance.
q: To whom thus Satan with contemptuous brow. Milton.
He told them with a masterly brow. Milton.

senses.d: The edge or projecting upper part of a steep place; as, the brow of a precipice; the brow of a hill.

Brow.etym: [OE. browe, bruwe, AS. br�; akin to AS. br�w, breáw, eyelid, OFries. brē, D. braauw, Icel. brā, br�n, OHG. prāwa, G. braue, OSlav. br�v�, Russ. brove, Ir. brai, Ir. & Gael. abhra, Armor. abrant, Gr. �, Skr. bhr�. Cf. Bray a bank, Bridge.]

senses.d: To bound to limit; to be at, or form, the edge of.
q: Tending my flocks hard by i' the hilly crofts That brow this bottom glade. Milton.

senses.d: Of a dark color, of various shades between black and red or yellow.
q: Cheeks brown as the oak leaves. Longfellow.

Brown.etym: [OE. brun, broun, AS. br�n; akin to D. bruin, OHG. br�n, Icel. br�nn, Sw. brun, Dan. bruun, G. braun, Lith. brunas, Skr. babhru. √93, 253. Cf. Bruin, Beaver, Burnish, Brunette.]

senses.d: A dark color inclining to red or yellow, resulting from the mixture of red and black, or of red, black, and yellow; a tawny, dusky hue.
To make brown or dusky.
q: A trembling twilight o'er welkin moves, Browns the dim void and darkens deep the groves. Barlow.

senses.d: To make brown by scorching slightly; as, to brown meat or flour.
To give a bright brown color to, as to gun barrels, by forming a thin coat of oxide on their surface.
To become brown.
To injure, as by a blow or collision, without laceration; to contuse; as, to bruise one's finger with a hammer; to bruise the bark of a tree with a stone; to bruise an apple by letting it fall.
To break; as in a mortar; to bray, as minerals, roots, etc.; to crush.
q: Nor bruise her flowerets with the armed hoofs. Shak.

Bruise.syn: To pulverize; bray; triturate; pound; contuse.
Bruise.etym: [OE. brusen, brisen, brosen, bresen, AS. brȳsan or fr. OF. bruiser, bruisier, bruser, to break, shiver, perh. from OHG. brochisōn. Cf. Break, v. t.]

senses.d: To fight with the fists; to box.
q: Bruising was considered a fine, manly, old English custom. Thackeray.

senses.d: An injury to the flesh of animals, or to plants, fruit, etc., with a blunt or heavy instrument, or by collision with some other body; a contusion; as, a bruise on the head; bruises on fruit.
q: From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises. Isa. i. 6.

senses.d: Report; rumor; fame.
q: The bruit thereof will bring you many friends. Shak.

senses.d: An abnormal sound of several kinds, heard on auscultation.

Bruit.etym: [OE. bruit, brut, noise, bruit, F. bruit, fr. LL. brugitus; cf. L. rugire to roar; perh. influenced by the source of E. bray to make a harsh noise, Armor. brud bruit.]

senses.d: To report; to noise abroad.
q: I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited. Shak.

senses.d: Not having sensation; senseless; inanimate; unconscious; without intelligence or volition; as, the brute earth; the brute powers of nature.
Not possessing reason, irrational; unthinking; as, a brute beast; the brute creation.
q: A creature . . . not prone And brute as other creatures, but endued With sanctity of reason. Milton.

senses.d: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of, a brute beast. Hence: Brutal; cruel; fierce; ferocious; savage; pitiless; as, brute violence.
q: The influence of capital and mere brute labor. Playfair.

senses.d: Having the physical powers predominating over the mental; coarse; unpolished; unintelligent.
q: A great brute farmer from Liddesdale. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: Rough; uncivilized; unfeeling.

Brute.etym: [F. brut, nasc., brute, fem., raw, rough, rude, brutish, L. brutus stupid, irrational: cf. It. & Sp. bruto.]

senses.d: An animal destitute of human reason; any animal not human; esp. a quadruped; a beast.
q: Brutes may be considered as either aëral, terrestrial, aquatic, or amphibious. Locke.

senses.d: A brutal person; a savage in heart or manners; as unfeeling or coarse person.
q: An ill-natured brute of a husband. Franklin.

senses.d: To report; to bruit.
Pertaining to, or resembling, a brute or brutes; of a cruel, gross, and stupid nature; coarse; unfeeling; unintelligent.
q: O, let all provocation Take every brutish shape it can devise. Leigh Hunt.
Man may . . . render himself brutish, but it is in vain that he would seek to take the rank and density of the brute. I. Taylor.

Brutish.syn: Insensible; stupid; unfeeling; savage; cruel; brutal; barbarous; inhuman; ferocious; gross; carnal; sensual; bestial.

senses.d: A vessel for drawing up water from a well, or for catching, holding, or carrying water, sap, or other liquids.
q: The old oaken bucket, the iron-bound bucket, The moss-covered bucket, which hung in the well. Wordsworth.

senses.d: A vessel (as a tub or scoop) for hoisting and conveying coal, ore, grain, etc.
One of the receptacles on the rim of a water wheel into which the water rushes, causing the wheel to revolve; also, a float of a paddle wheel.
The valved piston of a lifting pump.

Bucket.etym: [OE. boket; cf. AS. buc pitcher, or Corn. buket tub.]

senses.d: To draw or lift in, or as if in, buckets; as, to bucket water.
To pour over from a bucket; to drench.
To ride (a horse) hard or mercilessly.
To make, or cause to make (the recovery), with a certain hurried or unskillful forward swing of the body.

A device, usually of metal, consisting of a frame with one more movable tongues or catches, used for fastening things together, as parts of dress or harness, by means of a strap passing through the frame and pierced by the tongue.
A distortion bulge, bend, or kink, as in a saw blade or a plate of sheet metal.
A curl of hair, esp. a kind of crisp curl formerly worn; also, the state of being curled.
q: Earlocks in tight buckles on each side of a lantern face. W. Irving.
Lets his wig lie in buckle for a whole half year. Addison.

senses.d: A contorted expression, as of the face.
q: 'Gainst nature armed by gravity, His features too in buckle see. Churchill.

Buckle.etym: [OE. bocle buckle, boss of a shield, OF. bocle, F. boucle, boss of a shield, ring, fr. L. buccula a little cheek or mouth, dim. of bucca cheek; this boss or knob resembling a cheek.]

senses.d: To fasten or confine with a buckle or buckles; as, to buckle a harness.
To bend; to cause to kink, or to become distorted.
To prepare for action; to apply with vigor and earnestness; — generally used reflexively.
q: Cartwright buckled himself to the employment. Fuller.

senses.d: To join in marriage.

Buckle.etym: [OE. boclen, F. boucler. See Buckle, n.]

senses.d: To bend permanently; to become distorted; to bow; to curl; to kink.
q: Buckled with the heat of the fire like parchment. Pepys.

senses.d: To bend out of a true vertical plane, as a wall.
To yield; to give way; to cease opposing.
q: The Dutch, as high as they seem, do begin to buckle. Pepys.

senses.d: To enter upon some labor or contest; to join in close fight; to struggle; to contend.
q: The bishop was as able and ready to buckle with the Lord Protector as he was with him. Latimer.
In single combat thou shalt buckle with me. Shak.
To make our sturdy humor buckle thereto. Barrow.
Before buckling to my winter's work. J. D. Forbes.

senses.d: A kind of shield, of various shapes and sizes, worn on one of the arms (usually the left) for protecting the front of the body.
One of the large, bony, external plates found on many ganoid fishes.
A block of wood or plate of iron made to fit a hawse hole, or the circular opening in a half-port, to prevent water from entering when the vessel pitches.

Buckler.etym: [OE. bocler, OF. bocler, F. bouclier, a shield with a boss, from OF. bocle, boucle, boss. See Buckle, n.]

senses.d: To shield; to defend.
q: Can Oxford, that did ever fence the right, Now buckler falsehood with a pedigree? Shak.

senses.d: A small protuberance on the stem or branches of a plant, containing the rudiments of future leaves, flowers, or stems; an undeveloped branch or flower.
A small protuberance on certain low forms of animals and vegetables which develops into a new organism, either free or attached. See Hydra.

Bud.etym: [OE. budde; cf. D. bot, G. butze, butz, the core of a fruit, bud, LG. butte in hagebutte, hainbutte, a hip of the dog-rose, or OF. boton, F. bouton, bud, button, OF. boter to bud, push; all akin to E. beat. See Button.]

senses.d: To put forth or produce buds, as a plant; to grow, as a bud does, into a flower or shoot.
To begin to grow, or to issue from a stock in the manner of a bud, as a horn.
To be like a bud in respect to youth and freshness, or growth and promise; as, a budding virgin.

To graft, as a plant with another or into another, by inserting a bud from the one into an opening in the bark of the other, in order to raise, upon the budded stock, fruit different from that which it would naturally bear.
q: The apricot and the nectarine may be, and usually are, budded upon the peach; the plum and the peach are budded on each other. Farm. Dict.

senses.d: A cupboard or set of shelves, either movable or fixed at one side of a room, for the display of plate, china, etc., a sideboard.
q: Not when a gilt buffet's reflected pride Turns you from sound philosophy aside. Pope.

senses.d: A counter for refreshments; a restaurant at a railroad station, or place of public gathering.

Buffet.etym: [F. buffet, LL. bufetum; of uncertain origin; perh. fr. the same source as E. buffet a blow, the root meaning to puff, hence (cf. puffed up) the idea of ostentation or display.]

senses.d: A blow with the hand; a slap on the face; a cuff.
q: When on his cheek a buffet fell. Sir W. Scott.

senses.d: A blow from any source, or that which affects like a blow, as the violence of winds or waves; a stroke; an adverse action; an affliction; a trial; adversity.
q: Those planks of tough and hardy oak that used for yeas to brave the buffets of the Bay of Biscay. Burke.
Fortune's buffets and rewards. Shak.

senses.d: A small stool; a stool for a buffet or counter.
q: Go fetch us a light buffet. Townely Myst.

Buffet.etym: [OE. buffet, boffet, OF. buffet a slap in the face, a pair of bellows, fr. buffe blow, cf. F. bouffer to blow, puff; prob. akin to E. puff. For the meaning slap, blow, cf. F. soufflet a slap, souffler to blow. See Puff, v. i., and cf. Buffet sidebroad, Buffoon]

senses.d: To strike with the hand or fist; to box; to beat; to cuff; to slap.
q: They spit in his face and buffeted him. Matt. xxvi. 67.

senses.d: To affect as with blows; to strike repeatedly; to strive with or contend against; as, to buffet the billows.
q: The sudden hurricane in thunder roars, Buffets the bark, and whirls it from the shores. Broome.
You are lucky fellows who can live in a dreamland of your own, instead of being buffeted about the world. W. Black.

senses.d: To deaden the sound of (bells) by muffling the clapper.

Buffet.etym: [OE. buffeten, OF. buffeter. See the preceding noun.]

senses.d: To exercise or play at boxing; to strike; to smite; to strive; to contend.
q: If I might buffet for my love, or bound my horse for her favors, I could lay on like a butcher. Shak.

senses.d: To make one's way by blows or struggling.
q: Strove to buffet to land in vain. Tennyson.

senses.d: To erect or construct, as an edifice or fabric of any kind; to form by uniting materials into a regular structure; to fabricate; to make; to raise.
q: Nor aught availed him now To have built in heaven high towers. Milton.

senses.d: To raise or place on a foundation; to form, establish, or produce by using appropriate means.
q: Who builds his hopes in air of your good looks. Shak.

senses.d: To increase and strengthen; to increase the power and stability of; to settle, or establish, and preserve; — frequently with up; as, to build up one's constitution.
q: I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up. Acts xx. 32.

Build.syn: To erect; construct; raise; found; frame.
Build.etym: [OE. bulden, bilden, AS. byldan to build, fr. bold house; cf. Icel. bōl farm, abode, Dan. bol small farm, OSw. bol, böle, house, dwelling, fr. root of Icel. b�a to dwell; akin to E. be, bower, boor. √97.]

senses.d: To exercise the art, or practice the business, of building.
To rest or depend, as on a foundation; to ground one's self or one's hopes or opinions upon something deemed reliable; to rely; as, to build on the opinions or advice of others.
Form or mode of construction; general figure; make; as, the build of a ship.
One who builds; one whose occupation is to build, as a carpenter, a shipwright, or a mason.
q: In the practice of civil architecture, the builder comes between the architect who designs the work and the artisans who execute it. Eng. Cyc.

senses.d: The act of constructing, erecting, or establishing.
q: Hence it is that the building of our Sion rises no faster. Bp. Hall.

senses.d: The art of constructing edifices, or the practice of civil architecture.
q: The execution of works of architecture necessarily includes building; but building is frequently employed when the result is not architectural. Hosking.

senses.d: That which is built; a fabric or edifice constructed, as a house, a church, etc.
q: Thy sumptuous buildings and thy wife's attire Have cost a mass of public treasury. Shak.

senses.d: Shape; build; form of structure; as, the built of a ship.
Formed; shaped; constructed; made; — often used in composition and preceded by the word denoting the form; as, frigate-built, clipper-built, etc.
q: Like the generality of Genoese countrywomen, strongly built. Landor.

senses.d: The male of any species of cattle (Bovidæ); hence, the male of any large quadruped, as the elephant; also, the male of the whale.
One who, or that which, resembles a bull in character or action.
Taurus, the second of the twelve signs of the zodiac.
q: At last from Aries rolls the bounteous sun, And the bright Bull receives him. Thomson.

senses.d: One who operates in expectation of a rise in the price of stocks, or in order to effect such a rise. See 4th Bear, n., 5.

Bull.etym: [OE. bule, bul, bole; akin to D. bul, G. bulle, Icel. boli, Lith. bullus, Lett. bollis, Russ. vol'; prob. fr. the root of AS. bellan, E. bellow.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a bull; resembling a bull; male; large; fierce.
To be in heat; to manifest sexual desire as cows do.
To endeavor to raise the market price of; as, to bull railroad bonds; to bull stocks; to bull Lake Shore; to endeavor to raise prices in; as, to bull the market. See 1st Bull, n., 4.
A seal. See Bulla.

A letter, edict, or respect, of the pope, written in Gothic characters on rough parchment, sealed with a bulla, and dated “a die Incarnationis,” i.e., “from the day of the Incarnation.” See Apostolical brief, under Brief.
q: A fresh bull of Leo's had declared how inflexible the court of Rome was in the point of abuses. Atterbury.

senses.d: A grotesque blunder in language; an apparent congruity, but real incongruity, of ideas, contained in a form of expression; so called, perhaps, from the apparent incongruity between the dictatorial nature of the pope's bulls and his professions of humility.
q: And whereas the papist boasts himself to be a Roman Catholic, it is a mere contradiction, one of the pope's bulls, as if he should say universal particular; a Catholic schimatic. Milton.

Bull.etym: [OE. bulle, fr. L. bulla bubble, stud, knob, LL., a seal or stamp: cf. F. bulle. Cf. Bull a writing, Bowl a ball, Boil, v. i.]

senses.d: A young bull, or any male of the ox kind.
q: Take thy father's young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old. Judges vi. 25.

senses.d: An ox, steer, or stag.

Bullock.etym: [AS. bulluc a young bull. See Bull.]

senses.d: To bully.
q: She shan't think to bullock and domineer over me. Foote.

senses.d: A kind of large rush, growing in wet land or in water.

Bulrush.etym: [OE. bulrysche, bolroysche; of uncertain origin, perh. fr. bole stem + rush.]

senses.d: A rampart; a fortification; a bastion or outwork.
That which secures against an enemy, or defends from attack; any means of defense or protection.
q: The royal navy of England hath ever been its greatest defense, . . . the floating bulwark of our island. Blackstone.

senses.d: The sides of a ship above the upper deck.

Bulwark.etym: [Akin to D. bolwerk, G. bollwerk, Sw. bolwerk, Dan. bolvärk, bulvärk, rampart; akin to G. bohle plank, and werk work, defense. See Bole stem, and Work, n., and cf. Boulevard.]

senses.d: To fortify with, or as with, a rampart or wall; to secure by fortification; to protect.
q: Of some proud city, bulwarked round and armed With rising towers. Glover.

senses.d: A protuberance; a hunch; a knob or lump; a hump.
q: They will carry . . . their treasures upon the bunches of camels. Isa. xxx. 6.

senses.d: A collection, cluster, or tuft, properly of things of the same kind, growing or fastened together; as, a bunch of grapes; a bunch of keys.
A small isolated mass of ore, as distinguished from a continuous vein.

Bunch.etym: [Akin to OSw. & Dan. bunke heap, Icel. bunki heap, pile, bunga tumor, protuberance; cf. W. pwng cluster. Cf. Bunk.]

senses.d: To swell out into a bunch or protuberance; to be protuberant or round.
q: Bunching out into a large round knob at one end. Woodward.

senses.d: To form into a bunch or bunches.

A number of things bound together, as by a cord or envelope, into a mass or package convenient for handling or conveyance; a loose package; a roll; as, a bundle of straw or of paper; a bundle of old clothes.
q: The fable of the rods, which, when united in a bundle, no strength could bend. Goldsmith.

Bundle.etym: [OE. bundel, AS. byndel; akin to D. bondel, bundel, G. bündel, dim. of bund bundle, fr. the root of E. bind. See Bind.]

senses.d: To tie or bind in a bundle or roll.
To send off abruptly or without ceremony.
q: They unmercifully bundled me and my gallant second into our own hackney coach. T. Hook.

senses.d: To prepare for departure; to set off in a hurry or without ceremony.
To sleep on the same bed without undressing; — applied to the custom of a man and woman, especially lovers, thus sleeping.
q: Van Corlear stopped occasionally in the villages to eat pumpkin pies, dance at country frolics, and bundle with the Yankee lasses. W. Irving.

senses.d: Any rough or prickly envelope of the seeds of plants, whether a pericarp, a persistent calyx, or an involucre, as of the chestnut and burdock. Also, any weed which bears burs.
q: Amongst rude burs and thistles. Milton.
Bur and brake and brier. Tennyson.

senses.d: The thin ridge left by a tool in cutting or shaping metal. See Burr, n., 2.
A ring of iron on a lance or spear. See Burr, n., 4.
The lobe of the ear. See Burr, n., 5.
The sweetbread.
A clinker; a partially vitrified brick.
A small circular saw.
The round knob of an antler next to a deer's head.

Bur.etym: [OE. burre burdock; cf. Dan. borre, OSw. borra, burdock, thistle; perh. akin to E. bristle (burr- for burz-), or perh. to F. bourre hair, wool, stuff; also, according to Cotgrave, “the downe, or hairie coat, wherewith divers herbes, fruits, and flowers, are covered,” fr. L. burrae trifles, LL. rebur

senses.d: That which is borne or carried; a load.
q: Plants with goodly burden bowing. Shak.

senses.d: That which is borne with labor or difficulty; that which is grievous, wearisome, or oppressive.
q: Deaf, giddy, helpless, left alone, To all my friends a burden grown. Swift.

senses.d: The capacity of a vessel, or the weight of cargo that she will carry; as, a ship of a hundred tons burden.
The tops or heads of stream-work which lie over the stream of tin.
The proportion of ore and flux to fuel, in the charge of a blast furnace.
A fixed quantity of certain commodities; as, a burden of gad steel, 120 pounds.
A birth.

Burden.etym: [OE. burden, burthen, birthen, birden, AS. byrðen; akin to Icel. byrði, Dan. byrde, Sw. börda, G. bürde, OHG. burdi, Goth. baúrþei, fr. the root of E. bear, AS. beran, Goth. bairan. √92. See 1st Bear.]

senses.d: To encumber with weight (literal or figurative); to lay a heavy load upon; to load.
q: I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened. 2 Cor. viii. 13.

senses.d: To oppress with anything grievous or trying; to overload; as, to burden a nation with taxes.
q: My burdened heart would break. Shak.

senses.d: To impose, as a load or burden; to lay or place as a burden (something heavy or objectionable).
q: It is absurd to burden this act on Cromwell. Coleridge.

senses.d: The verse repeated in a song, or the return of the theme at the end of each stanza; the chorus; refrain. Hence: That which is often repeated or which is dwelt upon; the main topic; as, the burden of a prayer.
q: I would sing my song without a burden. Shak.

senses.d: The drone of a bagpipe.

Burden.etym: [OE. burdoun the bass in music, F. bourdon; cf. LL. burdo drone, a long organ pipe, a staff, a mule. Prob. of imitative origin. Cf. Bourdon.]

senses.d: A club.
Grievous to be borne; causing uneasiness or fatigue; oppressive.
q: The debt immense of endless gratitude So burdensome. Milton.

Burdensome.syn: Heavy; weighty; cumbersome; onerous; grievous; oppressive; troublesome.

senses.d: A grave; a tomb; a place of sepulture.
q: The erthe schook, and stoones weren cloven, and biriels weren opened. Wycliff .

senses.d: The act of burying; depositing a dead body in the earth, in a tomb or vault, or in the water, usually with attendant ceremonies; sepulture; interment.
q: Now to glorious burial slowly borne. Tennyson.

Burial.etym: [OE. buriel, buriels, grave, tomb, AS. byrgels, fr. byrgan to bury, and akin to OS. burgisli sepulcher.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, buries.
q: Till the buriers have buried it. Ezek. xxxix. 15.
And darkness be the burier of the dead. Shak.

senses.d: To consume with fire; to reduce to ashes by the action of heat or fire; — frequently intensified by up: as, to burn up wood.

To injure by fire or heat; to change destructively some property or properties of, by undue exposure to fire or heat; to scorch; to scald; to blister; to singe; to char; to sear; as, to burn steel in forging; to burn one's face in the sun; the sun burns the grass.

To perfect or improve by fire or heat; to submit to the action of fire or heat for some economic purpose; to destroy or change some property or properties of, by exposure to fire or heat in due degree for obtaining a desired residuum, product, or effect; to bake; as, to burn clay in making bricks or pottery; to burn wood so as to produce charcoal; to burn limestone for the lime.
To make or produce, as an effect or result, by the application of fire or heat; as, to burn a hole; to burn charcoal; to burn letters into a block.
To consume, injure, or change the condition of, as if by action of fire or heat; to affect as fire or heat does; as, to burn the mouth with pepper.
q: This tyrant fever burns me up. Shak.
This dry sorrow burns up all my tears.
When the cold north wind bloweth, . . . it devoureth the mountains, and burneth the wilderness, and consumeth the grass as fire. Ecclus. xliii. 20, 21.

senses.d: To apply a cautery to; to cauterize.
To cause to combine with oxygen or other active agent, with evolution of heat; to consume; to oxidize; as, a man burns a certain amount of carbon at each respiration; to burn iron in oxygen.

Burn.etym: [OE. bernen, brennen, v. t., early confused with beornen, birnen, v. i., AS. bærnan, bernan, v. t., birnan, v. i.; akin to OS. brinnan, OFries. barna, berna, OHG. brinnan, brennan, G. brennen, OD. bernen, D. branden, Dan. brænde, Sw. bränna, brinna, Icel. brenna, Goth. brinnan, brannjan (in comp.),

senses.d: To be of fire; to flame.
To suffer from, or be scorched by, an excess of heat.
q: Your meat doth burn, quoth I. Shak.

senses.d: To have a condition, quality, appearance, sensation, or emotion, as if on fire or excessively heated; to act or rage with destructive violence; to be in a state of lively emotion or strong desire; as, the face burns; to burn with fever.
q: Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way? Luke xxiv. 32.
The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne, Burned on the water. Shak.
Burning with high hope. Byron.
The groan still deepens, and the combat burns. Pope.
The parching air Burns frore, and cold performs the effect of fire. Milton.

senses.d: To combine energetically, with evolution of heat; as, copper burns in chlorine.
In certain games, to approach near to a concealed object which is sought.
A hurt, injury, or effect caused by fire or excessive or intense heat.
The operation or result of burning or baking, as in brickmaking; as, they have a good burn.
A disease in vegetables. See Brand, n., 6.
A small stream.
Burnished.
That burns; being on fire; excessively hot; fiery.
Consuming; intense; inflaming; exciting; vehement; powerful; as, burning zeal.
q: Like a young hound upon a burning scent. Dryden.

senses.d: The act of consuming by fire or heat, or of subjecting to the effect of fire or heat; the state of being on fire or excessively heated.
To cause to shine; to make smooth and bright; to polish; specifically, to polish by rubbing with something hard and smooth; as, to burnish brass or paper.
q: The frame of burnished steel, that east a glare From far, and seemed to thaw the freezing air. Dryden.
Now the village windows blaze, Burnished by the setting sun. Cunningham.

Burnish.etym: [OE. burnischen, burnissen, burnen, OF. burnir, brunir, to make brown, polish, F. brunir, fr. F. brun brown, fr. OHG. br�n; cf. MHG. briunen to make brown, polish. See Brown, a.]

senses.d: To shine forth; to brighten; to become smooth and glossy, as from swelling or filling out; hence, to grow large.
q: A slender poet must have time to grow, And spread and burnish as his brothers do. Dryden.
My thoughts began to burnish, sprout, and swell. Herbert.

senses.d: The effect of burnishing; gloss; brightness; luster.
Consumed with, or as with, fire; scorched or dried, as with fire or heat; baked or hardened in the fire or the sun.

To fly apart or in pieces; of break open; to yield to force or pressure, especially to a sudden and violent exertion of force, or to pressure from within; to explode; as, the boiler had burst; the buds will burst in spring.
q: From the egg that soon Bursting with kindly rupture, forth disclosed Their callow young. Milton.
No, no, my heart will burst, an if I speak: And I will speak, that so my heart may burst. Shak.

senses.d: To exert force or pressure by which something is made suddenly to give way; to break through obstacles or limitations; hence, to appear suddenly and unexpectedly or unaccountably, or to depart in such manner; — usually with some qualifying adverb or preposition, as forth, out, away, into, upon, through, etc.
q: Tears, such as angels weep, burst forth. Milton.
And now you burst (ah cruel!) from my arms. Pope.
A resolved villain Whose bowels suddenly burst out. Shak.
We were the first that ever burst Into that silent sea. Coleridge.
To burst upon him like an earthquake. Goldsmith.

Burst.etym: [OE. bersten, bresten, AS. berstan (pers. sing. berste, imp. sing. bærst, imp. pl. burston, p. p. borsten); akin to D. bersten, G. bersten, OHG. brestan, OS. brestan, Icel. bresta, Sw. brista, Dan. briste. Cf. Brast, Break.]

senses.d: To break or rend by violence, as by an overcharge or by strain or pressure, esp. from within; to force open suddenly; as, to burst a cannon; to burst a blood vessel; to burst open the doors.
q: My breast I'll burst with straining of my courage. Shak.

senses.d: To break.
q: You will not pay for the glasses you have burst? Shak.
He burst his lance against the sand below. Fairfax (Tasso).

senses.d: To produce as an effect of bursting; as, to burst a hole through the wall.
A sudden breaking forth; a violent rending; an explosion; as, a burst of thunder; a burst of applause; a burst of passion; a burst of inspiration.
q: Bursts of fox-hunting melody. W. Irving.

senses.d: Any brief, violent exertion or effort; a spurt; as, a burst of speed.
A sudden opening, as of landscape; a stretch; an expanse.
A rupture or hernia; a breach.
A borough; a manor; as, the Bury of St. Edmond's
A manor house; a castle.
q: To this very day, the chief house of a manor, or the lord's seat, is called bury, in some parts of England. Miege.

senses.d: To cover out of sight, either by heaping something over, or by placing within something, as earth, etc.; to conceal by covering; to hide; as, to bury coals in ashes; to bury the face in the hands.
q: And all their confidence Under the weight of mountains buried deep. Milton.

senses.d: Specifically: To cover out of sight, as the body of a deceased person, in a grave, a tomb, or the ocean; to deposit (a corpse) in its resting place, with funeral ceremonies; to inter; to inhume.
q: Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father. Matt. viii. 21.
I'll bury thee in a triumphant grave. Shak.

senses.d: To hide in oblivion; to put away finally; to abandon; as, to bury strife.
q: Give me a bowl of wine In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius. Shak.

Bury.syn: To intomb; inter; inhume; inurn; hide; cover; conceal; overwhelm; repress.
Bury.etym: [OE. burien, birien, berien, AS. byrgan; akin to beorgan to protect, OHG. bergan, G. bergen, Icel. bjarga, Sw. berga, Dan. bierge, Goth. baírgan. √95. Cf. Burrow.]

senses.d: A thicket, or place abounding in trees or shrubs; a wild forest.
A shrub; esp., a shrub with branches rising from or near the root; a thick shrub or a cluster of shrubs.
q: To bind a bush of thorns among sweet-smelling flowers. Gascoigne.

senses.d: A shrub cut off, or a shrublike branch of a tree; as, bushes to support pea vines.
A shrub or branch, properly, a branch of ivy (as sacred to Bacchus), hung out at vintners' doors, or as a tavern sign; hence, a tavern sign, and symbolically, the tavern itself.
q: If it be true that good wine needs no bush, 't is true that a good play needs no epilogue. Shak.

senses.d: The tail, or brush, of a fox.

Bush.etym: [OE. bosch, busch, buysch, bosk, busk; akin to D. bosch, OHG. busc, G. busch, Icel. būskr, būski, Dan. busk, Sw. buske, and also to LL. boscus, buscus, Pr. bosc, It. bosco, Sp. & Pg. bosque, F. bois, OF. bos. Whether the LL. or G. form is the original is uncertain; if the LL., it is perh. from the s

senses.d: To branch thickly in the manner of a bush.
To set bushes for; to support with bushes; as, to bush peas.
To use a bush harrow on (land), for covering seeds sown; to harrow with a bush; as, to bush a piece of land; to bush seeds into the ground.
A lining for a hole to make it smaller; a thimble or ring of metal or wood inserted in a plate or other part of machinery to receive the wear of a pivot or arbor.
A piece of copper, screwed into a gun, through which the venthole is bored.

Bush.etym: [D. bus a box, akin to E. box; or F. boucher to plug.]

senses.d: To furnish with a bush, or lining; as, to bush a pivot hole.
A dry measure, containing four pecks, eight gallons, or thirty-two quarts.
A vessel of the capacity of a bushel, used in measuring; a bushel measure.
q: Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed, and not to be set on a candlestick? Mark iv. 21.

senses.d: A quantity that fills a bushel measure; as, a heap containing ten bushels of apples.
A large indefinite quantity.
q: The worthies of antiquity bought the rarest pictures with bushels of gold, without counting the weight or the number of the pieces. Dryden.

senses.d: The iron lining in the nave of a wheel. In the United States it is called a box. See 4th Bush.

Bushel.etym: [OE. buschel, boischel, OF. boissel, bussel, boistel, F. boisseau, LL. bustellus; dim. of bustia, buxida (OF. boiste), fr. pyxida, acc. of L. pyxis box, Gr. �. Cf. Box.]

senses.d: To mend or repair, as men's garments; to repair garments.
Thick and spreading, like a bush.
Full of bushes; overgrowing with shrubs.
q: Dingle, or bushy dell, of this wild wood. Milton.

senses.d: That which busies one, or that which engages the time, attention, or labor of any one, as his principal concern or interest, whether for a longer or shorter time; constant employment; regular occupation; as, the business of life; business before pleasure.
q: Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business? Luke ii. 49.

senses.d: Any particular occupation or employment engaged in for livelihood or gain, as agriculture, trade, art, or a profession.
Financial dealings; buying and selling; traffic in general; mercantile transactions.
q: It seldom happens that men of a studious turn acquire any degree of reputation for their knowledge of business. Bp. Popteus.

senses.d: That which one has to do or should do; special service, duty, or mission.
q: The daughter of the King of France, On serious business, craving quick despatch, Importunes personal conference. Shak.
What business has the tortoise among the clouds? L'Estrange.

senses.d: Affair; concern; matter; — used in an indefinite sense, and modified by the connected words.
q: It was a gentle business, and becoming The action of good women. Shak.
Bestow Your needful counsel to our business. Shak.

senses.d: The position, distribution, and order of persons and properties on the stage of a theater, as determined by the stage manager in rehearsal.
Care; anxiety; diligence.

Business.syn: Affairs; concern; transaction; matter; engagement; employment; calling; occupation; trade; profession; vocation; office; duty.

senses.d: Engaged in some business; hard at work (either habitually or only for the time being); occupied with serious affairs; not idle nor at leisure; as, a busy merchant.
q: Sir, my mistress sends you word That she is busy, and she can not come. Shak.

senses.d: Constantly at work; diligent; active.
q: Busy hammers closing rivets up. Shak.
Religious motives . . . are so busy in the heart. Addison.

senses.d: Crowded with business or activities; — said of places and times; as, a busy street.
q: To-morrow is a busy day. Shak.

senses.d: Officious; meddling; foolish active.
q: On meddling monkey, or on busy ape. Shak.

senses.d: Careful; anxious.

Busy.syn: Diligent; industrious; assiduous; active; occupied; engaged.
Busy.etym: [OE. busi, bisi, AS. bysig; akin to D. bezig, LG. besig; cf. Skr. bhūsh to be active, busy.]

senses.d: To make or keep busy; to employ; to engage or keep engaged; to occupy; as, to busy one's self with books.
q: Be it thy course to busy giddy minds With foreign quarrels. Shak.

senses.d: One who officiously concerns himself with the affairs of others; a meddling person.
q: And not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not. 1 Tim. v. 13.

senses.d: Except with; unless with; without.
q: So insolent that he could not go but either spurning equals or trampling on his inferiors. Fuller.
Touch not the cat but a glove. Motto of the Mackintoshes.

senses.d: Except; besides; save.
q: Who can it be, ye gods! but perjured Lycon? E. Smith.

senses.d: Excepting or excluding the fact that; save that; were it not that; unless; — elliptical, for but that.
q: And but my noble Moor is true of mind . . . it were enough to put him to ill thinking. Shak.

senses.d: Otherwise than that; that not; — commonly, after a negative, with that.
q: It cannot be but nature hath some director, of infinite power, to guide her in all her ways. Hooker.
There is no question but the king of Spain will reform most of the abuses. Addison.

senses.d: Only; solely; merely.
q: Observe but how their own principles combat one another. Milton.
If they kill us, we shall but die. 2 Kings vii. 4.
A formidable man but to his friends. Dryden.

senses.d: On the contrary; on the other hand; only; yet; still; however; nevertheless; more; further; — as connective of sentences or clauses of a sentence, in a sense more or less exceptive or adversative; as, the House of Representatives passed the bill, but the Senate dissented; our wants are many, but quite of another kind.
q: Now abideth faith hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity. 1 Cor. xiii. 13.
When pride cometh, then cometh shame; but with the lowly is wisdom. Prov. xi. 2.
But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; . . . the lord of that servant will come in a day when he looketh not for him. Luke xii. 45, 46.

But.etym: [OE. bute, buten, AS. būtan, without, on the outside, except, besides; pref. be- + ūtan outward, without, fr. ūt out. Primarily, būtan, as well as ūt, is an adverb. √198. See By, Out; cf. About.]

senses.d: The outer apartment or kitchen of a two-roomed house; — opposed to ben, the inner room.
A limit; a boundary.
The end; esp. the larger or thicker end, or the blunt, in distinction from the sharp, end. See 1st Butt.
An officer in a king's or a nobleman's household, whose principal business it is to take charge of the liquors, plate, etc.; the head servant in a large house.
q: The butler and the baker of the king of Egypt. Gen. xl. 5.
Your wine locked up, your butler strolled abroad. Pope.

Butler.etym: [OE. boteler, F. bouteillier a bottle-bearer, a cupbearer, fr. LL. buticularius, fr. buticula bottle. See Bottle a hollow vessel.]

senses.d: The office of a butler.
A limit; a bound; a goal; the extreme bound; the end.
q: Here is my journey's end, here my butt And very sea mark of my utmost sail. Shak.

senses.d: The thicker end of anything. See But.
A mark to be shot at; a target.
q: The groom his fellow groom at butts defies, And bends his bow, and levels with his eyes. Dryden.

senses.d: A person at whom ridicule, jest, or contempt is directed; as, the butt of the company.
q: I played a sentence or two at my butt, which I thought very smart. Addison.

senses.d: A push, thrust, or sudden blow, given by the head of an animal; as, the butt of a ram.
A thrust in fencing.
q: To prove who gave the fairer butt, John shows the chalk on Robert's coat. Prior.

senses.d: A piece of land left unplowed at the end of a field.
q: The hay was growing upon headlands and butts in cornfields. Burrill.

senses.d: A joint where the ends of two objects come squarely together without scarfing or chamfering; — also called butt joint.
The joint where two planks in a strake meet.
A kind of hinge used in hanging doors, etc.; — so named because fastened on the edge of the door, which butts against the casing, instead of on its face, like the strap hinge; also called butt hinge.
The thickest and stoutest part of tanned oxhides, used for soles of boots, harness, trunks.
The hut or shelter of the person who attends to the targets in rifle practice.
q: Amen; and make me die a good old man! That's the butt end of a mother's blessing. Shak.

Butt.etym: [F. but butt, aim (cf. butte knoll), or bout, OF. bot, end, extremity, fr. boter, buter, to push, butt, strike, F. bouter; of German origin; cf. OHG. bōzan, akin to E. beat. See Beat, v. t.]

senses.d: To join at the butt, end, or outward extremity; to terminate; to be bounded; to abut.
q: And Barnsdale there doth butt on Don's well-watered ground. Drayton.

senses.d: To thrust the head forward; to strike by thrusting the head forward, as an ox or a ram. [See Butt, n.]
q: A snow-white steer before thine altar led, Butts with his threatening brows. Dryden.

Butt.etym: [OE. butten, OF. boter to push, F. bouter. See Butt an end, and cf. Boutade.]

senses.d: To strike by thrusting the head against; to strike with the head.
q: Two harmless lambs are butting one the other. Sir H. Wotton.

senses.d: A large cask or vessel for wine or beer. It contains two hogsheads.

Butt.etym: [F. botte, boute, LL. butta. Cf. Bottle a hollow vessel.]

senses.d: The common English flounder.
A detached low mountain, or high rising abruptly from the general level of the surrounding plain; — applied to peculiar elevations in the Rocky Mountain region.
q: The creek . . . passes by two remarkable buttes of red conglomerate. Ruxton.

senses.d: An oily, unctuous substance obtained from cream or milk by churning.

Any substance resembling butter in degree of consistence, or other qualities, especially, in old chemistry, the chlorides, as butter of antimony, sesquichloride of antimony; also, certain concrete fat oils remaining nearly solid at ordinary temperatures, as butter of cacao, vegetable butter, shea butter.

Butter.etym: [OE. botere, butter, AS. butere, fr. L. butyrum, Gr. βούτυρον; either fr. βούσ ox, cow + τυρόσ cheese; or, perhaps, of Scythian origin. Cf. Cow.]

senses.d: To cover or spread with butter.
q: I know what's what. I know on which side My bread is buttered. Ford.

senses.d: To increase, as stakes, at every throw or every game.
One who, or that which, butts.
The part at the back of the hip, which, in man, forms one of the rounded protuberances on which he sits; the rump.
The convexity of a ship behind, under the stern.
To acquire the ownership of (property) by giving an accepted price or consideration therefor, or by agreeing to do so; to acquire by the payment of a price or value; to purchase; — opposed to sell.
q: Buy what thou hast no need of, and ere long thou wilt sell thy necessaries. B. Franklin.

senses.d: To acquire or procure by something given or done in exchange, literally or figuratively; to get, at a cost or sacrifice; to buy pleasure with pain.
q: Buy the truth and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding. Prov. xxiii. 23.

Buy.etym: [OE. buggen, buggen, bien, AS. bycgan, akin to OS. buggean, Goth. bugjan.]

senses.d: To negotiate or treat about a purchase.
q: I will buy with you, sell with you. Shak.

senses.d: One who buys; a purchaser.
In the neighborhood of; near or next to; not far from; close to; along with; as, come and sit by me.
q: By foundation or by shady rivulet He sought them both. Milton.

senses.d: On; along; in traversing. Compare 5.
q: Long labors both by sea and land he bore. Dryden.
By land, by water, they renew the charge. Pope.

senses.d: Near to, while passing; hence, from one to the other side of; past; as, to go by a church.
Used in specifying adjacent dimensions; as, a cabin twenty feet by forty.
Against.
With, as means, way, process, etc.; through means of; with aid of; through; through the act or agency of; as, a city is destroyed by fire; profit is made by commerce; to take by force.

By.etym: [OE. bi, AS. bī, big, near to, by, of, from, after, according to; akin to OS. & OFries. bi, be, D. bij, OHG. bī, G. bei, Goth. bi, and perh. Gr. αμφἴ. E. prefix be- is orig. the same word. √203. See pref. Be-.]

senses.d: Near; in the neighborhood; present; as, there was no person by at the time.
Passing near; going past; past; beyond; as, the procession has gone by; a bird flew by.
Aside; as, to lay by; to put by.

Out of the common path; aside; — used in composition, giving the meaning of something aside, secondary, or incidental, or collateral matter, a thing private or avoiding notice; as, by-line, by-place, by-play, by-street. It was formerly more freely used in composition than it is now; as, by-business, by-concernment, by-design, by-interest, etc.
A secluded, private, or obscure way; a path or road aside from the main one.
A common saying; a proverb; a saying that has a general currency.
q: I knew a wise man that had it for a byword. Bacon.

senses.d: The object of a contemptuous saying.
q: Thou makest us a byword among the heathen. Ps. xliv. 14

senses.d: Lit., gate; — a title given to the founder of Babism, and taken from that of Bab-ud-Din, assumed by him.
